paper.name: Verse Literature
paper.author: Virgil
paper.title: Aeneid 4
paper.basis: OCR’s June 2022 verse paper and its 2022 to 2026 prose papers, mark schemes and examiners’ reports
paper.adviceNote: Drawn from OCR’s examiners’ reports on the literature papers (2024–2026), whose translations and 15-mark questions are set and marked in the same way, and from the commentaries on candidate answers.

questions.q: what do we learn about the queen’s condition?
points: she has been wounded for a long time (iamdudum saucia)
by a deep anxiety / love (gravi … cura)
she feeds the wound (vulnus alit)
in her veins (venis)
she is consumed by a hidden fire (caeco carpitur igni)

questions.q: what keeps coming back to Dido’s mind, and what effect does this have on her?
points: again and again (multa … multusque recursat)
his courage (viri virtus)
the honour of his family / line (gentis honos)
his face / looks (vultus) and his words (verbaque)
stay fixed in her heart (haerent infixi pectore)
her love / anxiety lets her body have no peaceful rest (nec placidam membris dat cura quietem)

questions.q: explain in your own words what Dido’s love is doing to her.
points: she cannot stop thinking of his face and his words (haerent infixi pectore vultus verbaque)
she cannot sleep / get any peaceful rest (nec placidam … dat cura quietem)
her body gets no relief (membris)

questions.q: what time is it, and how does Virgil describe it?
points: it is the next day (postera)
the sun was lighting the earth with his lamp (Phoebea lustrabat lampade terras)
dawn had cleared the dewy shadow from the sky (umentemque Aurora polo dimoverat umbram)

questions.q: what do we learn here about Dido and Anna?
points: Dido is hardly in her right mind (male sana)
she speaks to her sister (adloquitur … sororem)
her sister shares her every thought (unanimam)

questions.q: what does Dido tell Anna about her night?
points: dreams (insomnia)
terrify her (terrent)
and leave her uneasy / in suspense (me suspensam)

questions.q: who is this guest?
points: Aeneas

questions.q: what does Dido say about the newcomer?
points: he is new (novus)
he has come into their home (nostris successit sedibus)
as a guest (hospes)
he has a noble bearing / looks (quem sese ore ferens)
a brave heart (forti pectore)
and is strong in arms (armis)

questions.q: explain why Dido believes that Aeneas comes from the gods.
points: she really believes it (credo equidem)
and says her belief is not idle (nec vana fides)
that his family is divine (genus esse deorum)
because fear shows a low-born spirit (degeneres animos timor arguit), and he showed none

questions.q: what moves Dido about Aeneas’ story?
points: the fates by which he has been tossed about (quibus ille iactatus fatis)
the wars he told of (quae bella … canebat)
which he endured to the end (exhausta)

questions.q: describe Dido’s state at the start of Book 4.
points: she has long been wounded (iamdudum saucia)
she feeds the wound in her veins (vulnus alit venis)
she is consumed by a hidden fire (caeco carpitur igni)
Aeneas’ courage keeps returning to her mind (multa viri virtus animo … recursat)
and the honour of his family (gentis honos)
his face and words are fixed in her heart (haerent infixi pectore vultus verbaque)
she gets no peaceful rest (nec placidam membris dat cura quietem)

questions.q: when, and to whom, did Dido speak, and in what state was she?
points: the next day / at dawn (postera)
to her sister (sororem)
who shared her every thought (unanimam)
she was hardly in her right mind (male sana)

questions.q: what has Dido decided, and why?
points: it is fixed and immovable in her mind (animo fixum immotumque sederet)
that she would not join herself to anyone (ne cui me … vellem sociare)
in marriage (vinclo … iugali)
since her first love deceived her (primus amor deceptam … fefellit)
by his death (morte)
she has come to hate marriage (pertaesum thalami taedaeque)

questions.lemma: huic uni forsan potui succumbere culpae
questions.q: what does Dido admit here?
points: perhaps (forsan)
she could have given way (potui succumbere)
to this one fault (huic uni … culpae)

questions.q: why does Dido say she will not marry again?
points: her first love (primus amor)
deceived / cheated her (deceptam … fefellit)
by his death (morte)

questions.q: what does Dido confess to Anna?
points: she will admit it (fatebor enim)
since the death (post fata) of her poor husband Sychaeus (miseri … Sychaei coniugis)
and since her household gods were spattered with blood (sparsos … penates)
when her brother murdered him (fraterna caede)
this man alone (solus hic)
has moved her feelings (inflexit sensus)
and stirred her wavering heart (animumque labantem impulit)

questions.q: who was Sychaeus, and how had he died?
points: Dido’s first husband
he was murdered by her brother (Pygmalion, king of Tyre)
for his wealth

questions.q: explain what Dido recognises.
points: she recognises (agnosco)
the signs (vestigia)
of the old flame, the love she once felt for Sychaeus (veteris … flammae)

questions.q: what would Dido rather suffer than break her vow?
points: that the earth should gape open (tellus … dehiscat)
to its depths (ima)
or that the almighty father (pater omnipotens)
should drive her down with his thunderbolt (adigat me fulmine)
to the pale shadows of Erebus (pallentes umbras Erebi)
and deep night (noctemque profundam)
before she wrongs Honour (ante pudor quam te violo)
or breaks its laws (tua iura resolvo)

questions.q: who is meant?
points: Jupiter

questions.q: what does Dido say about her first husband?
points: he first joined her to himself (primus qui me sibi iunxit)
he has taken her love away with him (meos … amores abstulit)
let him keep it (habeat secum)
and guard it in his grave (servetque sepulcro)

questions.q: how does Dido’s speech end?
points: she finishes speaking (sic effata)
she fills her lap (sinum … implevit)
with welling tears (lacrimis … obortis)

questions.q: what does Dido reveal about her past and her present feelings?
points: her mind is fixed against remarrying (animo fixum immotumque)
her first love cheated her by his death (primus amor deceptam morte fefellit)
she has come to hate marriage (pertaesum thalami taedaeque)
perhaps she could give way (forsan potui succumbere)
her husband was murdered by her brother (fraterna caede)
this man alone has moved her feelings (solus hic inflexit sensus)
her heart was already wavering (animumque labantem)

questions.q: explain in your own words how Dido declares her loyalty to Sychaeus.
points: she would rather be swallowed by the earth (tellus … dehiscat)
or struck down by Jupiter’s thunderbolt (fulmine)
than break her vow of honour (quam te violo)
her love belongs to her first husband (meos … amores abstulit)
and he should keep it in his grave (servetque sepulcro)

questions.q: how does Anna address Dido?
points: as dearer to her sister than the light itself (luce magis dilecta sorori)
with deep affection (o … dilecta)

questions.q: what does Anna say Dido will miss if she stays alone?
points: she will be worn away (carpere)
alone and grieving (solane … maerens)
all through her youth (perpetua … iuventa)
she will never know sweet children (nec dulces natos)
or the rewards of love (Veneris … praemia)

questions.q: what does Anna suggest about the dead?
points: she asks whether Dido really believes (credis)
that ashes or the spirits in their graves (cinerem aut manes … sepultos)
care about such things (id … curare)

questions.q: how does Anna argue that this love is different from Dido’s past refusals?
points: she grants the point (esto)
no suitors moved Dido in her grief (aegram nulli … flexere mariti)
not in Libya, not before that in Tyre (non Libyae, non ante Tyro)
she rejected Iarbas (despectus Iarbas)
and the other chieftains (ductoresque alii) of Africa (Africa terra)
but now she would be fighting (pugnabis)
against a love that pleases her (placitone … amori)

questions.q: who was Iarbas?
points: a North African king who had wanted to marry Dido

questions.q: what does Anna ask Dido to remember?
points: whose lands she has settled in (quorum consederis arvis)
it has not occurred to her (nec venit in mentem)

questions.q: what dangers does Anna say surround Carthage?
points: the cities of the Gaetulians (Gaetulae urbes)
a people unconquerable in war (genus insuperabile bello)
the unbridled Numidians (Numidae infreni)
the inhospitable Syrtis (inhospita Syrtis)
a region deserted because of drought (deserta siti regio)
the Barcaeans, raging far and wide (lateque furentes Barcaei)
war rising from Tyre (bella Tyro surgentia)
the threats of her brother (germanique minas)

questions.q: describe the neighbours that Anna lists.
points: the Gaetulians, unconquerable in war (genus insuperabile bello)
the Numidians, without bridles / wild (Numidae infreni)
the Syrtis, which is inhospitable (inhospita Syrtis)
a region made desert by drought (deserta siti regio)
the Barcaeans, raging far and wide (lateque furentes Barcaei)
they hem Carthage in on both sides (hinc … hinc)

questions.q: what further dangers does Anna mention?
points: war rising from Tyre (bella Tyro surgentia)
the threats of Dido’s brother (germanique minas)
she says she need not even mention them (quid … dicam)

questions.q: who is Dido’s brother?
points: Pygmalion, king of Tyre (who murdered Sychaeus)

questions.q: what arguments does Anna use in her opening lines?
points: Dido is dearer to her than the light (luce magis dilecta)
Dido will grieve alone (solane … maerens)
all through her youth (perpetua … iuventa)
she will have no sweet children (nec dulces natos)
and none of the rewards of love (Veneris … praemia)
the dead do not care (id cinerem aut manes credis curare sepultos)

questions.q: what does Anna believe about the Trojans’ arrival?
points: she believes (reor) it happened with the gods as protectors (dis … auspicibus)
and with Juno’s favour (Iunone secunda)
the Trojan ships (Iliacas … carinas)
held this course with the wind (hunc cursum … vento tenuisse)

questions.q: whose goddess was Juno, and what was her attitude to the Trojans?
points: she was the patron goddess of Carthage
she was the enemy of the Trojans / of Aeneas

questions.q: what future does Anna predict for Carthage?
points: Dido will see a great city (quam tu urbem … cernes)
a kingdom will rise (quae surgere regna)
from such a marriage (coniugio tali)
with the Trojans’ arms alongside (Teucrum comitantibus armis)
Carthage’s glory will rise to great heights (Punica se quantis attollet gloria rebus)

questions.q: what does Anna tell Dido to do, and why will it work?
points: ask the gods for their goodwill (posce deos veniam)
once the sacrifices are favourably received (sacrisque litatis)
give herself over to hospitality (indulge hospitio)
weave reasons for delay (causasque innecte morandi)
while winter rages on the sea (dum pelago desaevit hiems)
and rainy Orion (aquosus Orion)
the ships are battered (quassataeque rates)
and the sky is unmanageable (non tractabile caelum)

questions.q: what does Anna advise Dido to do?
points: ask the gods for their goodwill (posce deos veniam)
after favourable sacrifices (sacrisque litatis)
give herself over to hospitality (indulge hospitio)
weave reasons for delay (causasque innecte morandi)

questions.q: explain why Anna thinks Aeneas will have to stay.
points: winter is raging on the sea (dum pelago desaevit hiems)
rainy Orion brings storms (aquosus Orion)
his ships are battered (quassataeque rates)
the sky is unmanageable (non tractabile caelum)

questions.q: what effect do Anna’s words have on Dido?
points: they set her heart ablaze (animum flammavit)
with a boundless passion (impenso … amore)
they gave hope (spemque dedit) to her wavering mind (dubiae menti)
they broke down her sense of honour (solvitque pudorem)

questions.q: explain in your own words what happened to Dido’s mind.
points: she was given hope (spemque dedit)
where her mind had been wavering (dubiae menti)
her sense of honour was broken down (solvitque pudorem)

questions.q: how does Anna argue that a marriage with Aeneas would benefit Carthage?
points: the gods protected the Trojans’ voyage (dis … auspicibus)
Juno favoured it (Iunone secunda)
the Trojan ships were guided here (hunc cursum … tenuisse)
Dido will see a great city (quam tu urbem)
a kingdom will rise (quae surgere regna)
from such a marriage (coniugio tali)
Trojan arms will march beside theirs (Teucrum comitantibus armis)
Carthage’s glory will rise (Punica … gloria)

questions.q: what do Dido and Anna do first?
points: they go to the shrines (delubra adeunt)
they seek peace / the gods’ favour at the altars (pacemque per aras exquirunt)
they sacrifice chosen sheep (mactant lectas … bidentes)
as custom demands (de more)

questions.q: to which gods do they sacrifice?
points: to Ceres the lawgiver (legiferae Cereri)
to Phoebus (Phoeboque)
to father Bacchus (patrique Lyaeo)
above all to Juno (Iunoni ante omnes)
who watches over the bonds of marriage (cui vincla iugalia curae)

questions.q: which god is meant?
points: Bacchus

questions.q: why do they sacrifice to Juno above all?
points: Juno watches over / cares for (cui … curae)
the bonds of marriage (vincla iugalia)
she is honoured before all the others (ante omnes)

questions.q: what had Dido sworn earlier about such bonds?
points: that she would never again join herself to anyone in marriage (after the death of Sychaeus)

questions.q: describe what Dido herself does at the sacrifice.
points: she does it herself (ipsa)
she holds the offering-dish in her right hand (tenens dextra pateram)
she pours it between the horns (media inter cornua fundit)
of a gleaming white cow (candentis vaccae)

questions.q: what else does Dido do during these rites?
points: she walks up and down before the faces of the gods (ante ora deum … spatiatur)
to the altars heaped with offerings (pingues … ad aras)
she begins the day afresh with gifts (instauratque diem donis)
she gazes eagerly into the opened breasts of the victims (pecudumque reclusis pectoribus inhians)
she consults the still-breathing entrails (spirantia consulit exta)

questions.q: describe how Dido examines the victims.
points: she gazes open-mouthed / eagerly (inhians)
into their opened breasts (reclusis pectoribus)
she consults the entrails (consulit exta)
which are still breathing (spirantia)

questions.q: what does Virgil say about seers?
points: their minds are ignorant / they know nothing (vatum ignarae mentes)

questions.q: explain in your own words what Virgil asks here.
points: what good are prayers (quid vota … iuvant)
what good are shrines (quid delubra iuvant)
to a woman who is mad with love (furentem)

questions.q: what is happening to Dido all the while?
points: a flame is eating at her (est … flamma)
her soft marrow (molles … medullas)
all the while (interea)
a silent wound lives on (tacitum vivit … vulnus)
beneath her heart (sub pectore)

questions.q: what comments does Virgil make about Dido’s situation?
points: the minds of seers are ignorant (vatum ignarae mentes)
prayers are of no use (quid vota … iuvant)
shrines are of no use (quid delubra iuvant)
she is mad with love (furentem)
a flame is eating her soft marrow (est molles flamma medullas)
a silent wound lives on beneath her heart (tacitum vivit sub pectore vulnus)

questions.q: describe how Dido and Anna seek the favour of the gods.
points: they go to the shrines (delubra adeunt)
they seek peace at the altars (pacemque per aras exquirunt)
they sacrifice chosen sheep (mactant lectas … bidentes)
as custom demands (de more)
to Ceres, Phoebus and Bacchus (Cereri Phoeboque patrique Lyaeo)
above all to Juno (Iunoni ante omnes)
who watches over marriage (cui vincla iugalia curae)

questions.q: what does Virgil tell us about Dido’s part in the sacrifices?
points: she takes part herself (ipsa)
she is at her most beautiful (pulcherrima Dido)
she holds the offering-dish in her right hand (tenens dextra pateram)
she pours it between the horns of a white cow (candentis vaccae media inter cornua fundit)
she walks up and down before the gods (ante ora deum … spatiatur)
she begins the day afresh with gifts (instauratque diem donis)
she gazes eagerly into the opened victims (reclusis pectoribus inhians)
she consults the still-breathing entrails (spirantia consulit exta)

questions.q: what does Virgil tell us about Dido’s state and behaviour?
points: she is burning (with love) (uritur)
she is unhappy / ill-starred (infelix Dido)
she wanders through the whole city (totaque vagatur urbe)
in her madness (furens)

questions.q: describe the deer and the shepherd in the simile.
points: a deer has been struck by an arrow (coniecta cerva sagitta)
she was off her guard (incautam)
the shepherd shot her from a distance (procul)
among the Cretan woods (nemora inter Cresia)
he was hunting with his weapons (pastor agens telis)
he left the flying arrow in her (liquitque volatile ferrum)
without knowing it (nescius)

questions.q: what does the deer do, and why can she not escape?
points: she runs in flight (illa fuga … peragrat)
through the forests and glades (silvas saltusque)
of Dicte (Dictaeos)
the deadly arrow is still fixed in her side (haeret lateri letalis harundo)

questions.q: why does Virgil describe the shepherd as nescius?
points: he was simply out hunting with his weapons (pastor agens telis)
he left his arrow in the deer (liquitque volatile ferrum)
he does not know that he has hit her (nescius)

questions.q: what does Dido do with Aeneas during the day?
points: she leads Aeneas with her (Aenean secum … ducit)
through the heart of the city (media … per moenia)
she shows off her Phoenician wealth (Sidoniasque ostentat opes)
and the city already built (urbemque paratam)

questions.q: what happens when Dido tries to speak?
points: she begins to speak (incipit effari)
she stops (resistit)
in mid-sentence (mediaque in voce)

questions.q: what does Dido do as the day ends?
points: as the day fades (labente die)
she calls for the same banquet again (eadem … convivia quaerit)
she begs to hear again (iterum … audire … exposcit)
the sufferings of Troy (Iliacosque … labores)
in her madness (demens)
she hangs again on the speaker’s lips (pendetque iterum narrantis ab ore)

questions.q: what sufferings are meant, and when had Dido first heard of them?
points: the fall / sack of Troy
and the Trojans’ wanderings that followed
Aeneas told the story at Dido’s banquet (in Books 2 and 3)

questions.q: when does the next scene take place?
points: after they have parted (post ubi digressi)
when the moon dims her light (lumenque obscura … luna premit)
when the setting stars urge sleep (suadentque cadentia sidera somnos)

questions.q: describe Dido’s behaviour once she is alone.
points: she grieves (maeret)
alone (sola)
in the empty house (domo … vacua)
she lies on the couch he has left (stratisque relictis incubat)

questions.q: what does Dido do while Aeneas is away from her?
points: she hears him and sees him (auditque videtque)
though both are apart (absens absentem)
she holds Ascanius on her lap (gremio Ascanium … detinet)
captivated by his likeness to his father (genitoris imagine capta)
to see whether she can deceive (si fallere possit)
a love she cannot speak of (infandum … amorem)

questions.q: why does Dido keep Ascanius on her lap?
points: she is captivated by his likeness to his father (genitoris imagine capta)
she hopes she can deceive / cheat (si fallere possit)
her unspeakable love (infandum … amorem)

questions.q: who was Ascanius?
points: Aeneas’ young son (also called Iulus)

questions.q: how does Virgil show in these lines that Dido’s love is harming her?
points: she is burning (uritur)
she is unhappy / ill-starred (infelix Dido)
she wanders through the whole city (totaque vagatur urbe)
she is mad (furens)
she is like a deer struck by an arrow (coniecta cerva sagitta)
caught off guard (incautam)
she runs through the woods (fuga silvas saltusque peragrat)
the deadly arrow stays fixed in her side (haeret lateri letalis harundo)

questions.q: what has happened to the building of Carthage?
points: the towers already begun no longer rise (non coeptae adsurgunt turres)
the young men no longer practise arms (non arma iuventus exercet)
they no longer prepare the harbours (portusve … parant)
or battlements to keep the city safe in war (propugnacula bello tuta)
the work hangs interrupted (pendent opera interrupta)
the huge menacing walls stand idle (minaeque murorum ingentes)
and the crane that reached the sky (aequataque machina caelo)

questions.q: what are the people of Carthage no longer doing?
points: building up the towers they had begun (non coeptae adsurgunt turres)
practising with arms (non arma iuventus exercet)
preparing harbours (portusve … parant)
preparing battlements to keep them safe in war (propugnacula bello tuta)

questions.q: describe the state of the building works.
points: the work hangs unfinished (pendent opera interrupta)
the huge menacing walls (minaeque murorum ingentes)
the crane that rose level with the sky (aequataque machina caelo)

questions.q: what did Juno realise about Dido?
points: she sensed (persensit)
that Dido was gripped (teneri)
by such a sickness / plague (tali … peste)
her reputation no longer stood in the way (nec famam obstare)
of her passion / madness (furori)

questions.q: who is meant?
points: Juno

questions.q: what did Juno notice, and what did she then do?
points: as soon as she noticed (simul ac … persensit)
Dido was gripped by such a sickness (tali … peste teneri)
her reputation was no obstacle to her passion (nec famam obstare furori)
she approached Venus (adgreditur Venerem)
with these words (talibus … dictis)

questions.q: what does Juno say Venus and Cupid have achieved?
points: splendid glory (egregiam vero laudem)
rich spoils (spolia ampla)
you and your boy (tuque puerque tuus)
a great and memorable pair of gods (magnum et memorabile numen)
one woman (una … femina) has been overcome (victa)
by the trickery of two gods (dolo divum … duorum)

questions.q: explain why Juno’s praise of Venus is not meant seriously.
points: they have only overcome one woman (una … femina victa)
and it took two gods to do it (divum … duorum)
using trickery (dolo)

questions.q: who is meant, and what had he done to Dido?
points: Cupid
he took the form of Ascanius (in Book 1)
and made Dido fall in love with Aeneas

questions.q: what does Juno say she has noticed?
points: it has not escaped her (nec me adeo fallit)
Venus is afraid (veritam te)
of Juno’s walls (moenia nostra)
she has held the homes of Carthage in suspicion (suspectas habuisse domos Karthaginis)

questions.q: what questions does Juno ask?
points: where will it end (quis erit modus)
what is the point now (quo nunc)
of such a great contest (certamine tanto)

questions.q: what does Juno say to Venus?
points: she speaks of the splendid glory (egregiam vero laudem)
and rich spoils Venus and Cupid have won (spolia ampla refertis)
one woman has been overcome (una … femina victa)
by the trickery of two gods (dolo divum … duorum)
it has not escaped her (nec me adeo fallit)
that Venus fears her walls (veritam te moenia nostra)
and suspects the homes of Carthage (suspectas habuisse domos Karthaginis)
she asks where it will end (quis erit modus)
and what such a contest is for (quo nunc certamine tanto)

questions.q: what does Juno propose?
points: a lasting peace (pacem aeternam)
an agreed marriage (pactosque hymenaeos)
in place of their quarrel (quin potius)

questions.q: what does Juno say Venus has achieved?
points: she has what she wanted (habes … quod … petisti)
with her whole heart (tota … mente)
Dido is burning with love (ardet amans Dido)
the madness has gone right through her bones (traxitque per ossa furorem)

questions.q: what arrangement does Juno suggest?
points: they should rule this people in common (communem hunc … populum … regamus)
with equal authority (paribusque … auspiciis)
Dido may serve a Trojan husband (liceat Phrygio servire marito)
and hand over her Tyrians as a dowry (dotalesque … Tyrios permittere)
into Venus’ control (tuae … dextrae)

questions.q: who is meant?
points: Aeneas

questions.q: what did Venus realise about Juno’s offer?
points: she realised (sensit)
that Juno had spoken with false intent (simulata mente locutam)
to divert the kingdom of Italy (regnum Italiae … averteret)
to the shores of Libya (Libycas … oras)

questions.q: to which city does Juno want to turn the kingdom aside?
points: Carthage

questions.q: how does Venus reply at first?
points: who would be mad enough (quis talia demens)
to refuse such an offer (abnuat)
or prefer to go to war with Juno (tecum malit contendere bello)

questions.q: what condition does Venus add?
points: if only fortune follows (si modo … fortuna sequatur)
what Juno proposes (quod memoras factum)

questions.q: what is Venus unsure about?
points: she is uncertain about the fates (fatis incerta feror)
whether Jupiter wants (si Iuppiter … velit)
one city (unam esse … urbem)
for the Tyrians and the exiles from Troy (Tyriis … Troiaque profectis)
or would approve of the peoples mingling (miscerive probet populos)
or of treaties joining them (foedera iungi)

questions.q: what does Venus tell Juno to do?
points: Juno is Jupiter’s wife (tu coniunx)
it is right for her (tibi fas)

questions.q: what does Dido command the Tyrians to do?
points: hound with their hatred (exercete odiis)
Aeneas’ line (stirpem)
and his whole race to come (genus omne futurum)
send this as a gift to her ashes (cinerique haec mittite nostro munera)
there must be no love between the peoples (nullus amor populis)
and no treaties (nec foedera sunto)

questions.q: what does Dido call for?
points: an avenger (ultor)
to rise up (exoriare aliquis)
from her bones (nostris ex ossibus)
to hound (sequare)
the Trojan settlers (Dardanios … colonos)
with fire and sword (face … ferroque)

questions.q: who are meant by the Dardanian settlers?
points: the Trojans (Aeneas’ people, settling in Italy)

questions.q: describe the conflict Dido calls for.
points: now or in time to come (nunc olim)
whenever the strength arises (quocumque dabunt se tempore vires)
shore against shore (litora litoribus contraria)

no love and no treaties between the peoples (nullus amor populis nec foedera sunto)

to hound the Trojan settlers with fire and sword (face Dardanios ferroque sequare colonos)
now or in time to come (nunc olim)
shore against shore, sea against sea, weapon against weapon (litora litoribus contraria)

essays.q: how does Virgil present Dido’s love as a sickness and a torment?
points: Dido has already been suffering for a long time when the book opens
her love is a wound that she keeps feeding instead of letting it heal
it is a hidden fire that eats her away from inside
Aeneas’ courage and family keep returning to her thoughts
his face and words are fixed in her heart, and she cannot sleep
a calm, bright dawn comes while she has had no rest
she is hardly in her right mind when she speaks to Anna
her first words are about dreams that terrify her
features: at regina gravi iamdudum saucia cura: the book opens with the queen already wounded; iamdudum shows the torment has gone on all night, and gravi … cura makes her love a heavy anxiety
vulnus alit venis: paradox of feeding a wound instead of tending it, so love is a sickness she keeps alive in her own blood
caeco carpitur igni: fire imagery with harsh alliteration of c; the hidden fire eats her away from inside like a fever
multa viri virtus animo multusque recursat gentis honos: repetition of multus and the v alliteration of viri virtus show his qualities returning to torment her mind again and again
haerent infixi pectore vultus verbaque: infixi recalls an arrow driven in, and the enjambment of verbaque makes his words cling on into the next line as they cling in her heart
nec placidam membris dat cura quietem: cura returns from line 1 to enclose the sentence, and the denial of rest shows love as a physical illness that robs her body of sleep
postera Phoebea lustrabat lampade terras: the calm, bright dawn contrasts with the sleepless darkness of Dido's mind, so her torment stands out
cum sic unanimam adloquitur male sana sororem: male sana, literally ‘badly sane’, presents her as sick in mind before she speaks
quae me suspensam insomnia terrent: exclamation; her sleepless nights terrify her and leave her in suspense, the symptoms of a disturbed and suffering mind

essays.q: how does Virgil show that Dido is dazzled by Aeneas?
points: Dido speaks to her sister at dawn, hardly in her right mind
she has been kept awake and terrified by dreams
she bursts out with questions about the new guest in her home
she admires his bearing, his courage and his strength in arms
she is sure that he is descended from the gods
she argues that his lack of fear proves his noble birth
she pities him for the fates that have tossed him about
she is moved by the wars he has told of
features: cum sic unanimam adloquitur male sana sororem: male sana warns that Dido's judgement is already unsound as she begins to praise Aeneas
quae me suspensam insomnia terrent: the opening exclamation shows her in a state of breathless excitement, kept awake by him
quis novus hic nostris successit sedibus hospes: rhetorical question; novus and the emphatic hic show her wonder at this stranger who has entered her home
quem sese ore ferens, quam forti pectore et armis: exclamations with anaphora (quem … quam) and a rising tricolon of his looks, courage and arms show how dazzled she is
credo equidem, nec vana fides, genus esse deorum: she insists, with the parenthesis nec vana fides, that he must be descended from gods; her admiration becomes almost worship
degeneres animos timor arguit: a short maxim used to prove his noble birth; she argues like a general to justify her admiration
heu, quibus ille iactatus fatis: the exclamation heu shows pity mixed with admiration for the sufferings he has endured
quae bella exhausta canebat: canebat makes his story sound like an epic song; she is enchanted by him as storyteller as well as warrior

essays.q: how does Virgil make this a vivid opening to Book 4?
points: the book opens with the queen already wounded by love
her love is pictured as a wound and a hidden fire
Aeneas’ qualities, face and words fill her thoughts
she spends a sleepless night while a calm dawn rises
she turns to her sister, who shares her every thought
she pours out her feelings in a rush of exclamations and questions
she praises Aeneas as divine, brave and noble
she pities him for his sufferings and the wars he has endured
features: at regina gravi iamdudum saucia cura: at plunges us into a new scene, and iamdudum opens in the middle of her suffering, a dramatic start
vulnus alit venis et caeco carpitur igni: two vivid images of love, a wound and a hidden fire, introduced together; the alliteration of c makes the fire bite
haerent infixi pectore vultus verbaque: infixi pictures his face and words driven into her heart, and the enjambment of verbaque makes them cling on
nec placidam membris dat cura quietem: cura encloses the opening sentence and the line ends on the rest she cannot have, so we see a sleepless queen
postera Phoebea lustrabat lampade terras umentemque Aurora polo dimoverat umbram: grand epic description of dawn, its light set against the darkness of her night
cum sic unanimam adloquitur male sana sororem: the shift into direct speech brings us close to her disturbed mind, flagged by male sana
quae me suspensam insomnia terrent: Dido's first words are an exclamation of fear and sleeplessness, which makes her voice urgent and immediate
quem sese ore ferens, quam forti pectore et armis: breathless exclamations and a rising tricolon of praise let us hear how dazzled she is
heu, quibus ille iactatus fatis! quae bella exhausta canebat: two further exclamations end the passage on a high pitch of emotion and pity

essays.q: how does Virgil show the conflict in Dido’s mind?
points: Dido insists that her decision not to remarry is fixed and immovable
she explains that her first love cheated her by dying
she says that she has come to hate marriage
yet she admits that she could perhaps have given way to this one fault
she confesses to Anna that Aeneas alone has moved her
she recalls the murder of Sychaeus by her brother
her heart is described as already wavering
she recognises the signs of the love she once felt
features: si mihi non animo fixum immotumque sederet: the near-synonyms fixum immotumque stress how firm she claims her resolve is, so its collapse shows the strength of the conflict
ne cui me vinclo vellem sociare iugali: marriage pictured as a chain or yoke, something she fears yet is drawn towards
primus amor deceptam morte fefellit: deceptam … fefellit doubles the idea of betrayal; loyalty to her first love pulls against the new
si non pertaesum thalami taedaeque fuisset: two ‘if not’ clauses hold back the main verb, so the conflict is built into the sentence; the alliteration of t stresses her weariness of marriage
huic uni forsan potui succumbere culpae: she admits in potui that she could have given in, while forsan and huic uni try to make it small; calling love a culpa shows her guilt
miseri post fata Sychaei coniugis: miseri shows her continuing pity and love for Sychaeus, which makes the new feelings painful to admit
solus hic inflexit sensus animumque labantem impulit: her heart is a wall already slipping, and the run-over to impulit enacts the push Aeneas has given it
agnosco veteris vestigia flammae: fire imagery; the ‘old flame’ she once felt for Sychaeus is the very feeling that now draws her to Aeneas, so both loves meet in one line

essays.q: how does Virgil make Dido’s oath of loyalty to Sychaeus powerful?
points: Dido confesses that Aeneas alone has moved her since Sychaeus’ death
she recalls the bloody murder of her husband by her brother
she recognises the old flame of love returning
she would rather the earth swallowed her
or that Jupiter struck her down to the underworld with his thunderbolt
she addresses Honour directly and swears not to break its laws
she insists that her love belongs to Sychaeus in his grave
her speech ends with her lap full of tears
features: Anna, fatebor enim: the confession comes first, so the oath that follows is a struggle against what she has just admitted, which adds to its force
sparsos fraterna caede penates: the vivid picture of blood on the household gods recalls the crime that took Sychaeus, giving the oath its painful background

sed mihi vel tellus optem prius ima dehiscat vel pater omnipotens adigat me fulmine ad umbras: two terrible alternatives, from below and from above, linked by vel … vel, show how solemnly she means it
pater omnipotens adigat me fulmine: she calls on Jupiter's thunderbolt, the punishment for oath-breakers, so the oath is sworn before the highest god
ad umbras, pallentes umbras Erebi noctemque profundam: umbras is repeated and expanded into a picture of the dark underworld, making the curse on herself chillingly vivid
ante, pudor, quam te violo aut tua iura resolvo: apostrophe to her own sense of honour as if to a goddess; breaking the oath becomes a kind of sacrilege
ille meos, primus qui me sibi iunxit, amores abstulit: the emphatic ille and the enjambment of abstulit stress that her love belongs to Sychaeus alone
ille habeat secum servetque sepulcro: repeated ille and the alliteration of s close the oath with finality: her love is to stay with him in the grave
sic effata sinum lacrimis implevit obortis: the oath ends in floods of tears, showing how much it costs her to swear it

essays.q: how does Virgil present Dido’s struggle between her new love and her loyalty to Sychaeus?
points: she claims her resolve not to remarry is fixed
her first love was taken from her by death
she admits she might have given way to this one fault
she confesses that Aeneas alone has stirred her wavering heart
she recognises the signs of her old love
she swears she would rather die than break her vow
she declares that Sychaeus keeps her love in his grave
she ends in tears, which shows how weak her defences are
features: si mihi non animo fixum immotumque sederet: the pairing fixum immotumque presents her loyalty as unshakeable, setting up the struggle that follows
primus amor deceptam morte fefellit: her first love is personified as having cheated her by dying; loyalty to it is mixed with hurt
huic uni forsan potui succumbere culpae: after two conditional clauses she admits in potui that she could give way; culpa shows that she already feels the new love as a betrayal
solus hic inflexit sensus animumque labantem impulit: solus hic stresses that only Aeneas has moved her, and the enjambment of impulit shows her wavering heart pushed over
agnosco veteris vestigia flammae: fire imagery joins the two loves: what she feels for Aeneas is the old flame she once felt for Sychaeus
sed mihi vel tellus optem prius ima dehiscat: the strong adversative sed swings her back to loyalty, so the speech enacts the struggle
ante, pudor, quam te violo aut tua iura resolvo: apostrophe to pudor; loyalty to Sychaeus becomes a sacred duty she would rather die than break
ille meos, primus qui me sibi iunxit, amores abstulit; ille habeat secum servetque sepulcro: anaphora of ille points firmly to Sychaeus as she tries to hand her love back to him in the grave
sic effata sinum lacrimis implevit obortis: her speech ends in tears, which suggests that the struggle is far from won

essays.q: how does Virgil make Anna’s arguments persuasive?
points: Anna begins with deep affection for her sister
she asks whether Dido will waste her youth in lonely grief
she reminds her of the children and love she would miss
she dismisses the idea that the dead care
she concedes Dido’s past refusals of suitors such as Iarbas
she asks whether Dido will fight a love that pleases her
she lists the hostile peoples surrounding Carthage
she ends with the threat of war from Tyre and from Dido’s brother
features: o luce magis dilecta sorori: Anna opens with hyperbolic affection, loving Dido more than life, which disarms her before the argument begins

solane perpetua maerens carpere iuventa: a rhetorical question, so Dido seems to persuade herself; carpere echoes the wasting of line 2 and perpetua … iuventa stresses how much of her youth would be lost
nec dulces natos Veneris nec praemia noris: nec … nec pairs children and love, the two things a widow gives up, an appeal to her heart
id cinerem aut manes credis curare sepultos: a blunt, dismissive question that reduces Sychaeus to dust and shades, undercutting Dido's oath
esto: aegram nulli quondam flexere mariti: the concession esto grants Dido's past refusals only to turn them against her
non Libyae, non ante Tyro; despectus Iarbas: anaphora of non sweeps quickly through her rejections so Anna can reach her key point
placitone etiam pugnabis amori: the decisive question; placito stresses that this love is welcome, and pugnabis makes resistance sound like a pointless war against herself

hinc Gaetulae urbes, genus insuperabile bello, et Numidae infreni cingunt: anaphora of hinc and the frightening descriptions of warlike neighbours make Carthage seem surrounded and in need of a protector
quid bella Tyro surgentia dicam germanique minas: praeteritio; by saying she will not mention the threat from Tyre and Dido's brother, Anna ends on the most personal danger of all

essays.q: how does Virgil present Anna’s appeal to Dido’s feelings?
points: Anna calls Dido dearer to her than the light
she pictures Dido worn away by lonely grief
she stresses that Dido is still young
she offers the prospect of sweet children and love
she suggests that the dead do not care
she grants that Dido has refused other suitors
she argues that resisting a welcome love is a pointless fight
she turns to remind Dido of the land she has settled in
features: o luce magis dilecta sorori: Anna begins with hyperbolic affection, an emotional appeal that comes before any argument
solane perpetua maerens carpere iuventa: she pictures Dido alone, grieving and wasting away; sola placed first stresses her loneliness
perpetua … iuventa: Anna stresses that Dido is still young, so a lifetime of mourning seems a waste
nec dulces natos Veneris nec praemia noris: the pairing of sweet children and the rewards of love appeals to what Dido longs for, made sweeter by dulces
id cinerem aut manes credis curare sepultos: a scornful rhetorical question that reduces the dead Sychaeus to ashes, freeing Dido from guilt
esto: aegram nulli quondam flexere mariti: aegram sympathises with her past grief before turning it into a reason to change
despectus Iarbas ductoresque alii: Anna flatters Dido by recalling the powerful suitors she has scorned, so Aeneas becomes the one man worthy of her
placitone etiam pugnabis amori: the climax of the emotional appeal; Anna names Dido's love as welcome and asks why she should fight it
nec venit in mentem quorum consederis arvis: a further question that asks Dido to look at her situation, gently shifting from feeling to fear

essays.q: how does Virgil make Anna’s political argument for the marriage convincing?
points: Anna reminds Dido whose lands she has settled in
she lists warlike and wild peoples on every side
even the land and the coast are hostile
she hints at war from Tyre and Dido’s brother
she claims the gods and Juno guided the Trojan ships
she imagines the great city and kingdom that would rise
Trojan arms would march beside Carthage’s
Carthage’s glory would be raised to great heights
features: nec venit in mentem quorum consederis arvis: a rhetorical question that makes Dido face the dangers of her position for herself
hinc Gaetulae urbes, genus insuperabile bello: anaphora of hinc begins a list of enemies; insuperabile bello exaggerates their threat to make protection seem essential
et Numidae infreni cingunt et inhospita Syrtis: polysyndeton and the image of riders ‘without bridles’ make the neighbours wild and lawless, and cingunt shows Carthage surrounded
hinc deserta siti regio lateque furentes Barcaei: even the land is hostile, and late furentes makes the Barcaeans rage far and wide; enjambment carries the threat over the line
quid bella Tyro surgentia dicam germanique minas: praeteritio raises the danger from Tyre and Dido's own brother while claiming to pass over it
dis equidem auspicibus reor et Iunone secunda: the language of official auspices presents the Trojans' arrival as approved by the gods and by Juno, Carthage's own goddess
hunc cursum Iliacas vento tenuisse carinas: the epic adjective Iliacas and the idea that the wind steered them make the alliance seem fated
quam tu urbem, soror, hanc cernes, quae surgere regna coniugio tali: exclamations of a city and kingdom rising; coniugio tali, placed at the start of the line, calls the match a marriage
Teucrum comitantibus armis Punica se quantis attollet gloria rebus: Trojan arms set beside Carthaginian glory turn a love affair into a policy for defence and greatness

essays.q: how does Virgil make Anna’s vision of the future persuasive?
points: Anna believes the gods and Juno brought the Trojans to Carthage
she imagines the great city and kingdom that would rise
she already calls the match a marriage
Trojan arms would support Carthage and raise its glory
she makes the next steps sound easy: prayers and hospitality
she suggests weaving reasons to delay Aeneas
the winter storms will keep the Trojan ships in port
her words set Dido’s heart ablaze and break down her honour
features: dis equidem auspicibus reor et Iunone secunda: Anna claims the gods and Juno as supporters; the language of auspices gives her vision divine approval
hunc cursum Iliacas vento tenuisse carinas: the epic phrasing and the wind that brought the ships make the future seem planned by fate
quam tu urbem, soror, hanc cernes, quae surgere regna: exclamatory clauses with quam … quae make Dido see the future as if before her eyes; the direct address soror makes it personal
coniugio tali: placed at the start of the line, the word ‘marriage’ is presented as natural, the step on which the whole vision depends
Teucrum comitantibus armis Punica se quantis attollet gloria rebus: Trojan arms and Punic glory are set side by side, and attollet pictures that glory rising like a great building
tu modo posce deos veniam, sacrisque litatis: tu modo makes the path to this future sound easy: only prayer and sacrifice are needed
indulge hospitio causasque innecte morandi: love is dressed up as the duty of a host, and innecte suggests weaving a web of reasons to keep Aeneas
dum pelago desaevit hiems et aquosus Orion, quassataeque rates, dum non tractabile caelum: a tricolon of practical reasons, with repeated dum, makes delay seem sensible
his dictis impenso animum flammavit amore: fire imagery shows the vision working at once, setting Dido's heart ablaze

essays.q: how does Virgil show Anna’s words overcoming Dido’s resistance?
points: Anna paints a glorious picture of the city Dido will see
she speaks of the match as a marriage
she promises Trojan support and Carthaginian glory
she tells Dido she need only ask the gods for goodwill
she presents love as the duty of hospitality
she advises weaving reasons for delay
the winter weather makes delay seem sensible
Dido is set ablaze, given hope, and loses her sense of honour
features: quam tu urbem, soror, hanc cernes, quae surgere regna coniugio tali: Anna's excited exclamations paint a future Dido can almost see, and call the match a marriage
Punica se quantis attollet gloria rebus: the promise of Carthaginian glory appeals to Dido the founder and queen
tu modo posce deos veniam: tu modo shrinks the obstacle: all Dido has to do is ask the gods' pardon
indulge hospitio causasque innecte morandi: two short commands; indulge hospitio makes love sound respectable, and innecte pictures a web of excuses to hold Aeneas
dum pelago desaevit hiems et aquosus Orion: heavy d alliteration conveys winter storms that give Dido a ready excuse
quassataeque rates, dum non tractabile caelum: practical details of damaged ships and an unmanageable sky remove her last objections
his dictis impenso animum flammavit amore: the fire imagery and impenso show Anna's words inflaming Dido at once
spemque dedit dubiae menti solvitque pudorem: a tricolon of effects; hope is given, doubt overcome and pudor ‘loosened’, the very honour she swore to keep in line 27

essays.q: how does Virgil present Anna as a skilful persuader?
points: she claims the support of the gods and of Juno
she makes the Trojans’ arrival seem divinely guided
she excites Dido with a vision of a great city and kingdom
she names the match a marriage
she presents Aeneas as a powerful ally for Carthage
she makes the next steps sound simple
she dresses up love as hospitality
she gives practical reasons why Aeneas must stay through the winter
features: dis equidem auspicibus reor et Iunone secunda: Anna begins by claiming divine support, choosing Juno, the goddess Dido honours most
hunc cursum Iliacas vento tenuisse carinas: she presents chance as fate, so Aeneas' arrival seems to demand a response
quam tu urbem, soror, hanc cernes, quae surgere regna: vivid exclamations and the affectionate soror appeal to Dido's imagination and to their bond
coniugio tali: Anna slips in the word ‘marriage’ at the start of the line as if it were already agreed
Teucrum comitantibus armis Punica se quantis attollet gloria rebus: she switches to politics, offering Trojan military support and Carthaginian glory, so love seems also to serve the state
tu modo posce deos veniam, sacrisque litatis: a series of easy instructions; tu modo makes the plan simple and respectable
indulge hospitio causasque innecte morandi: skilful euphemism presents love as hospitality, and innecte suggests a cunning plan to delay Aeneas
dum pelago desaevit hiems et aquosus Orion, quassataeque rates, dum non tractabile caelum: a closing tricolon of practical reasons, with anaphora of dum, gives Dido a ready excuse

essays.q: how does Virgil show that Dido’s prayers and sacrifices cannot help her?
points: Dido and Anna go from shrine to shrine seeking the gods’ favour
they sacrifice chosen sheep in the proper way, as custom demands
they offer to several gods, and above all to Juno, who watches over marriage, which shows what Dido wants
Dido herself, at her most beautiful, pours the offering between the horns of a white cow
she walks before the gods and keeps beginning the day afresh with gifts
she stares into the opened victims and searches the still-breathing entrails for a sign
the narrator cries out that seers know nothing: prayers and shrines are no use to a woman mad with love
all the while a flame eats her marrow and a silent wound lives in her heart
features: principio delubra adeunt pacemque per aras exquirunt: the sisters begin correctly with the gods, but pacem suggests the inner peace Dido cannot find there
mactant lectas de more bidentes: de more stresses that every rite is done properly, which makes its failure all the more striking
legiferae Cereri Phoeboque patrique Lyaeo, Iunoni ante omnes: polysyndeton shows her trying god after god, and the list climaxes on Juno, goddess of marriage
cui vincla iugalia curae: the same bonds of marriage she swore never to enter (line 16) are now what she prays for, so the rites serve her passion
pecudumque reclusis pectoribus inhians spirantia consulit exta: inhians shows her staring hungrily into the opened victims; their opened breasts mirror her own wounded heart
heu, vatum ignarae mentes: the narrator breaks in with heu and an exclamation: even those who read the signs cannot see that Dido is beyond help
quid vota furentem, quid delubra iuvant: two rhetorical questions with anaphora of quid declare the prayers and shrines useless; furentem names her madness
est molles flamma medullas interea: est (‘eats’) and the fire imagery show love consuming her to the marrow while she worships; interea sets the fire against the rites
tacitum vivit sub pectore vulnus: the wound of line 2 returns, silent and alive, with soft v alliteration; no sacrifice can heal it

essays.lemma: ipsa tenens … haeret lateri letalis harundo
essays.q: how does Virgil present Dido as a victim of her love?
points: Dido performs the rites herself, eager for a sign from the gods
she stares hungrily into the opened victims and their still-breathing entrails
the narrator says her prayers and the shrines are no help to a woman mad with love
a flame eats at her marrow and a silent wound lives in her heart
she burns and wanders through the whole city in her madness
she is like a deer struck by an arrow while off her guard
the shepherd who shot her does not know he has hit her
she runs through the woods, but the deadly arrow stays fixed in her side
features: ipsa tenens dextra pateram pulcherrima Dido: Dido at her most beautiful, doing the rites herself, which makes her coming suffering more pitiable
pecudumque reclusis pectoribus inhians spirantia consulit exta: the still-breathing victims she stares into foreshadow her own death and link her with the sacrificed
heu, vatum ignarae mentes! quid vota furentem, quid delubra iuvant: the narrator's exclamation and questions show that nothing can save her: she is helpless before her love
est molles flamma medullas interea et tacitum vivit sub pectore vulnus: fire and wound imagery show love attacking her from inside, an enemy she cannot fight
uritur infelix Dido: uritur placed first makes her burning define her, and infelix, her recurring epithet, marks her as doomed
totaque vagatur urbe furens: enjambment spreads her aimless wandering across the line as it spreads through the city; furens shows that she is no longer in control
qualis coniecta cerva sagitta: simile of the wounded deer, a helpless hunted animal; the word order frames cerva with the arrow, pinning her as the arrow does
pastor agens telis liquitque volatile ferrum nescius: the unknowing shepherd stands for Aeneas; nescius, held back to the next line, stresses that she suffers from a wound he did not mean to give
illa fuga silvas saltusque peragrat Dictaeos: the s alliteration conveys her frantic, breathless flight, which cannot rid her of the arrow
haeret lateri letalis harundo: the simile ends on the arrow still fixed in her, and letalis looks ahead to her death; the l sounds slow the line to a close

essays.q: how does Virgil make this a vivid account of Dido’s sacrifices?
points: the sisters go from shrine to shrine and from altar to altar
chosen sheep are sacrificed to a list of gods, ending with Juno, goddess of marriage
Dido is pictured holding the offering-dish and pouring it between the horns of a gleaming white cow
she paces before the faces of the gods to altars heaped with offerings
she offers gifts all day long
she gazes open-mouthed into the opened victims and consults their still-breathing entrails
the narrator breaks in with a cry about the ignorance of seers and the uselessness of prayers
the scene ends with the hidden flame and the silent wound inside her
features: principio delubra adeunt pacemque per aras exquirunt: the sisters move from shrine to shrine and altar to altar, a busy, crowded opening
mactant lectas de more bidentes: precise ritual detail of chosen victims slaughtered in the proper way brings the scene before our eyes
legiferae Cereri Phoeboque patrique Lyaeo, Iunoni ante omnes: a list of gods joined by polysyndeton, building to Juno, gives the scene a sense of mounting effort

ipsa tenens dextra pateram pulcherrima Dido candentis vaccae media inter cornua fundit: a precise picture of Dido pouring the libation between the white heifer's horns; ipsa and pulcherrima focus our eyes on her
aut ante ora deum pingues spatiatur ad aras: spatiatur, ‘walks to and fro’, shows her restless movement before the statues of the gods
instauratque diem donis: she renews the day with gifts, sacrificing again and again, which adds to the sense of a long, frantic ritual
pecudumque reclusis pectoribus inhians spirantia consulit exta: gruesome detail of the opened breasts and still-breathing entrails, with inhians showing her open-mouthed stare
heu, vatum ignarae mentes! quid vota furentem, quid delubra iuvant: the narrator's sudden exclamation and questions break the scene, turning description into pathos
est molles flamma medullas interea et tacitum vivit sub pectore vulnus: the passage ends on vivid fire and wound imagery, the hidden reality beneath the public rites

essays.q: how does Virgil make this a vivid picture of Dido’s love for Aeneas?
points: Dido burns and wanders through the whole city in her madness
she is compared to a deer struck by an arrow among the Cretan woods
the shepherd shot her from a distance and does not know he has hit her
she runs through the forests, but the deadly arrow stays in her side
she leads Aeneas through the city and shows off her wealth and her new city
she begins to speak and stops in mid-sentence
as the day fades she calls for the same banquet again
she begs to hear the story of Troy again and hangs on his every word
features: uritur infelix Dido: the verb of burning comes first, before her name, so passion defines Dido before anything else, and the epithet infelix makes her love a misfortune from the start
totaque vagatur urbe furens: enjambment carries urbe furens over the line break, so her restless wandering spills across the verse as it spills through the whole city; furens makes her love a madness
qualis coniecta cerva sagitta: the simile turns her love into a wound; the word order sets the deer between coniecta and sagitta, so the arrow pins her in place
pastor agens telis liquitque volatile ferrum nescius: the unknowing shepherd stands for Aeneas, unaware of the harm he has done; nescius is held over to the start of the line for emphasis
fuga silvas saltusque peragrat: the sibilance of s gives a rushing, breathless sound to the deer's flight, picturing Dido's frantic restlessness
haeret lateri letalis harundo: the simile ends on the arrow still fixed in her side; the alliteration of l slows the line, and letalis makes the love fatal

nunc media Aenean secum per moenia ducit … nunc eadem labente die convivia quaerit: the anaphora of nunc divides her days into restless phases, so we see her swinging from one way of keeping Aeneas near to another
Sidoniasque ostentat opes urbemque paratam: ostentat, ‘shows off’, gives a vivid picture of Dido displaying her city to win him
incipit effari mediaque in voce resistit: the broken-off sentence is a striking detail of her confusion in his presence

Iliacosque iterum demens audire labores exposcit pendetque iterum narrantis ab ore: the repeated iterum and the word demens show her obsession; she literally ‘hangs’ on his lips, a vivid image of complete absorption

essays.q: how does Virgil show the effect of Aeneas on Dido by day and by night?
points: by day she leads Aeneas through the city and shows him her wealth and her city
she starts to speak to him and breaks off in mid-sentence
in the evening she calls for the same feast again
in her madness she begs to hear about the sufferings of Troy again and hangs on his words
when they part at night, and the stars urge sleep, she grieves alone in the empty house
she lies on the couch he has left
though they are apart, she hears and sees him
she holds Ascanius on her lap because he looks like his father, hoping to deceive her love
features: nunc media Aenean secum per moenia ducit: by day Dido keeps Aeneas at her side (secum), leading him through the heart of her city
Sidoniasque ostentat opes urbemque paratam: ostentat, ‘shows off’, shows her trying to win him with her wealth and her new city
incipit effari mediaque in voce resistit: she breaks off in mid-sentence, a vivid detail of how his presence unsettles her
nunc eadem labente die convivia quaerit: the anaphora of nunc and the repeated feast (eadem) show each day ending in the same way, organised around him

Iliacosque iterum demens audire labores exposcit pendetque iterum narrantis ab ore: the doubled iterum and demens show an obsessive need to hear him again; pendet pictures her hanging on his every word
lumenque obscura vicissim luna premit suadentque cadentia sidera somnos: the slow, quiet description of nightfall, with soft s sounds, sets the calm of the world against Dido's sleeplessness
sola domo maeret vacua stratisque relictis incubat: sola and vacua stress her loneliness at night; enjambment leaves incubat isolated at the start of the line, as she lies on the couch he has left
illum absens absentem auditque videtque: the polyptoton absens absentem sets the two apart lovers side by side, and the double -que shows that she still hears and sees him though he is gone
gremio Ascanium genitoris imagine capta detinet: she holds the boy because he looks like his father; the enjambment of detinet stresses how she clings to this substitute
infandum si fallere possit amorem: infandum, ‘unspeakable’, marks her love as something she cannot admit, and the line ends on amorem, the cause of it all

essays.lemma: post ubi digressi … aequataque machina caelo
essays.q: how does Virgil show the damage Dido’s love is doing, to herself and to her city?
points: after the evening ends and the moon and stars bring the night, Dido is left alone
she grieves in the empty house and lies on the couch Aeneas has left
she hears and sees him although he is not there
she holds Ascanius because he looks like his father, trying to deceive a love she cannot speak of
in the city the towers no longer rise
the young men no longer train with weapons, and the harbours and battlements are not prepared
the building work hangs unfinished, with the huge walls and the tall crane standing idle
features: lumenque obscura vicissim luna premit suadentque cadentia sidera somnos: the peaceful description of night, with soft sibilance and slow rhythm, sets the rest of the world against the harm Dido is suffering
sola domo maeret vacua stratisque relictis incubat: the adjectives sola and vacua stress her isolation and grief; enjambment isolates incubat, as she lies helplessly on the couch he has left
illum absens absentem auditque videtque: polyptoton and the double -que show a mind haunted by him, seeing and hearing him when he is not there
gremio Ascanium genitoris imagine capta detinet: capta, ‘captured’, shows her love as a captivity; she clings to the child as a substitute for his father
infandum si fallere possit amorem: infandum marks her love as shameful and unspeakable, a hurt she tries in vain to deceive

non coeptae adsurgunt turres, non arma iuventus exercet: the anaphora of non lists the work that has stopped item by item, so the damage to the city builds up; coeptae recalls that it was once under way
portusve aut propugnacula bello tuta parant: the defences that should keep Carthage safe in war are left unprepared, so Dido's love leaves her city exposed
pendent opera interrupta: the unfinished buildings ‘hang’ in mid-air, as Dido hung on Aeneas' words (pendet, line 79), so her state of mind is mirrored in her city
minaeque murorum ingentes aequataque machina caelo: the alliteration of m and the hyperbole of a crane level with the sky make the halted work all the more striking, power standing idle

essays.q: how does Virgil present Juno as cunning and persuasive?
points: Carthage has come to a standstill: no towers rise, no young men train, the work hangs unfinished
Juno, Jupiter’s wife, sees that Dido is gripped by a sickness and has stopped caring for her reputation
she goes straight to Venus with a prepared speech
she mockingly praises Venus and Cupid for their glory and spoils
she points out that two gods have used trickery to defeat one woman
she shows that she knows Venus fears and suspects Carthage
she ends by asking where the quarrel will end, preparing for her offer
features: non coeptae adsurgunt turres, non arma iuventus exercet: the anaphora of non sets out the city's paralysis first, the situation Juno will exploit
tali persensit peste teneri: Juno sees Dido's love as a pestis, a sickness, and watches for her chance before she acts
nec famam obstare furori: Juno notes that reputation no longer restrains Dido's passion, the weakness her scheme relies on
cara Iovis coniunx … Saturnia: the grand titles stress her standing as Jupiter's wife and Saturn's daughter, and cara is ironic for a goddess about to scheme behind her husband's back
talibus adgreditur Venerem Saturnia dictis: adgreditur is a word for making an attack, so her speech is presented as a planned assault on Venus
egregiam vero laudem et spolia ampla refertis: heavy sarcasm in the language of a military triumph belittles Venus' victory and puts her on the defensive
tuque puerque tuus magnum et memorabile numen: the parenthesis mocks Venus and Cupid with grand language, a cunning way to shame them into a deal
una dolo divum si femina victa duorum est: una and duorum frame the line, one woman against two gods, and dolo is placed pointedly, so the victory sounds as shameful as possible

nec me adeo fallit veritam te moenia nostra suspectas habuisse domos: she shows that she understands Venus' fears, which makes her seem shrewd; moenia nostra reminds Venus that Carthage is Juno's city
sed quis erit modus, aut quo nunc certamine tanto?: the closing rhetorical questions make her sound weary of the quarrel and ready to compromise, preparing persuasively for her offer

essays.q: how does Virgil show Juno mocking Venus?
points: Juno acts as soon as she sees Dido gripped by a sickness of love
she sees that Dido’s reputation no longer holds back her passion
she approaches Venus with a speech
she speaks of the splendid glory and rich spoils Venus and Cupid have won
she calls Venus and her son a great and memorable pair of gods
she says the victory is one woman beaten by the trickery of two gods
she says she knows Venus fears Carthage and suspects its homes
she asks where the contest will end
features: tali persensit peste teneri: Juno sees Dido's love as a pestis, a sickness, a sign of the harm Venus has done that Juno will now throw back at her
cara Iovis coniunx … Saturnia: the grand titles set Juno up as the senior goddess, Jupiter's wife and Saturn's daughter, speaking down to Venus
talibus adgreditur Venerem Saturnia dictis: adgreditur, ‘attacks’, frames her speech as an assault on Venus
egregiam vero laudem et spolia ampla refertis: vero is heavily ironic, and the language of triumph and spoils mocks a victory won over one woman
tuque puerque tuus magnum et memorabile numen: the parenthesis is sarcastic; the alliteration of m in magnum et memorabile inflates the praise to make it ridiculous, and puer tuus belittles Cupid
una dolo divum si femina victa duorum est: una and duorum frame the line, setting one mere woman against two gods; the heavy d sounds and dolo stress that they won by trickery
nec me adeo fallit veritam te moenia nostra: the litotes nec me fallit lets Juno say coolly that she has seen through Venus' fears
suspectas habuisse domos Karthaginis altae: the grand phrase Karthaginis altae mocks Venus' fear of Juno's lofty city
sed quis erit modus, aut quo nunc certamine tanto?: the rhetorical questions turn the mockery into weary condescension, as if Venus' quarrel were childish

essays.q: how does Virgil present the consequences of Dido’s passion?
points: the towers that had been begun no longer rise
the young men no longer practise with weapons
the harbours and battlements for war are left unprepared
the work hangs interrupted, with huge walls and a crane as high as the sky standing idle
Juno sees that Dido is gripped by a sickness
Dido’s reputation no longer stands in the way of her passion
Juno turns the situation into a quarrel with Venus over the two gods who have overcome one woman
features: non coeptae adsurgunt turres, non arma iuventus exercet: the anaphora of non lists what has stopped, so the consequences for the city build up item by item; coeptae recalls work once begun
portusve aut propugnacula bello tuta parant: harbours and battlements are left unprepared, so Dido's passion leaves her city defenceless in war
pendent opera interrupta: the unfinished buildings ‘hang’, as Dido hung on Aeneas' words, so the city mirrors her paralysis
minaeque murorum ingentes aequataque machina caelo: the alliteration of m and the hyperbole of a crane as high as the sky stress how much has been abandoned
tali persensit peste teneri: love is a pestis, a sickness or ruin, which presents her passion as destructive and spreading
nec famam obstare furori: fama and furor are set side by side: her reputation, the next casualty, no longer restrains her madness
talibus adgreditur Venerem Saturnia dictis: Dido's passion now draws in the gods, as Juno moves to exploit it
una dolo divum si femina victa duorum est: una and duorum frame the line, one woman overcome by two gods, showing Dido as the victim of forces beyond her

essays.q: how does Virgil make Juno’s proposal persuasive?
points: Juno opens by mocking the glory Venus and Cupid have won over one woman
she shows she knows Venus fears and suspects Carthage
she asks where their quarrel will end
she offers instead a lasting peace and an agreed marriage
she says Venus already has what she wanted, as Dido burns with love
she suggests they rule the people together with equal authority
Dido would serve a Trojan husband and hand over her people as a dowry
features: egregiam vero laudem et spolia ampla refertis: Juno opens with sarcasm in the language of triumph, putting Venus on the defensive before she makes her offer
una dolo divum si femina victa duorum est: una and duorum frame the line, so Venus' victory sounds shameful and a settlement more attractive
nec me adeo fallit veritam te moenia nostra: by showing she understands Venus' fears, Juno makes herself seem reasonable and well informed
sed quis erit modus, aut quo nunc certamine tanto?: the rhetorical questions make continued conflict seem pointless and prepare for her proposal
quin potius pacem aeternam pactosque hymenaeos exercemus?: the offer is framed as a friendly question; the alliteration of p links peace and pact, so the deal sounds neat and settled
habes tota quod mente petisti: flattery tells Venus she has already won, so agreeing seems the natural next step
ardet amans Dido traxitque per ossa furorem: fire and fever imagery shows Dido's love is beyond cure, so Juno presents the marriage as merely accepting what has happened
communem hunc ergo populum paribusque regamus auspiciis: ergo makes her offer sound logical; the language of shared rule and equal authority makes it seem fair
dotalesque tuae Tyrios permittere dextrae: Juno offers the whole Tyrian people as a dowry into Venus' hand, a generous-sounding bargain

essays.q: how does Virgil present the two goddesses as scheming against each other?
points: Juno proposes a lasting peace and an agreed marriage
she tells Venus she already has what she wanted, since Dido burns with love
she suggests they rule the people together with equal authority
Dido would serve a Trojan husband and hand over her Tyrians as a dowry
Venus sees that Juno is lying, to divert the kingdom of Italy to Libya
Venus pretends to welcome the offer and asks who would refuse it
she adds the condition that fortune must allow it and claims to be uncertain about the fates
she hands the task back to Juno, as Jupiter’s wife, and agrees to follow her lead
features: quin potius pacem aeternam pactosque hymenaeos exercemus?: Juno's proposal is framed as a friendly question; the alliteration of p makes the deal sound neat, hiding her real purpose
habes tota quod mente petisti: she flatters Venus that she has already won, a tactic to win her agreement
communem hunc ergo populum paribusque regamus auspiciis: the language of equal shares disguises a plan to rule the people from Carthage
liceat Phrygio servire marito: servire, ‘to be a slave’, and the slightly scornful Phrygio let Juno's contempt show through her apparent generosity
sensit enim simulata mente locutam: the parenthesis tells the reader directly that Juno is lying, so we watch the rest as a game between two schemers
quo regnum Italiae Libycas averteret oras: the aside reveals Juno's true aim, to divert the destined kingdom of Italy to Libya; the two places are set against each other
quis talia demens abnuat aut tecum malit contendere bello?: Venus answers with polite rhetorical questions, appearing to agree while committing to nothing
si modo quod memoras factum fortuna sequatur: si modo is her escape clause: she agrees only if fortune allows, which she knows it will not
sed fatis incerta feror: Venus feigns uncertainty about the fates, a polite fiction that protects her own plans

tu coniunx, tibi fas animum temptare precando. perge, sequar: the emphatic tu and tibi hand responsibility back to Juno, and the brisk asyndeton of perge, sequar ends the exchange with Venus apparently compliant

essays.q: how does Virgil show Venus outwitting Juno?
points: Venus realises that Juno has spoken with false intent
she sees that Juno wants to divert the kingdom of Italy to Libya
she replies politely, asking who would be mad enough to refuse such an offer
or to prefer war with Juno
she adds the condition that fortune must follow what Juno proposes
she claims to be uncertain whether Jupiter wants one city for Tyrians and Trojans
she tells Juno that, as Jupiter’s wife, it is her place to sound him out
she ends by telling Juno to lead on and promising to follow
features: sensit enim simulata mente locutam: the parenthesis shows Venus seeing through Juno at once; simulata mente exposes the pretence she must now outwit
quo regnum Italiae Libycas averteret oras: the aside states Juno's real aim, to divert Italy's kingdom to Libya, so we know exactly what Venus is guarding against
sic contra est ingressa Venus: contra marks her reply as a counter-move in the contest
quis talia demens abnuat: Venus answers with a courteous rhetorical question, apparently eager while agreeing to nothing; demens flatters Juno that refusal would be madness
aut tecum malit contendere bello?: she claims to want no war with Juno, a humble pose that disarms her rival
si modo quod memoras factum fortuna sequatur: si modo, ‘if only’, is her escape clause: she agrees in principle, but only if fortune allows
sed fatis incerta feror: Venus pretends not to know the will of fate, a polite fiction that lets Jupiter's decision do her work

unam esse velit Tyriis urbem Troiaque profectis, miscerive probet populos aut foedera iungi: the tricolon lists every way of uniting the peoples without accepting any, turning Juno's offer into a string of doubtful conditions
tu coniunx, tibi fas animum temptare precando: the emphatic tu and tibi pass the task of persuading Jupiter back to Juno
perge, sequar: the short asyndeton and the half-line close the speech briskly, as Venus appears to follow while leaving the outcome to fate

essays.q: how does Virgil present Juno’s plan?
points: Juno takes the task on herself and tells Venus to listen while she explains briefly how it can be done
she knows that Aeneas and Dido mean to go hunting together at sunrise the next day
she will pour down a black storm mixed with hail while the hunters are busy setting their nets
she will fill the whole sky with thunder
the companions will scatter and be hidden in the darkness
Dido and the Trojan leader will come to the same cave
Juno will be there and, with Venus’ agreement, will join them in a lasting marriage and call it their wedding
Venus agrees without opposing her and smiles, having seen through the trick
features: mecum erit iste labor: mecum comes first, so Juno takes the plan on herself at once

nunc qua ratione quod instat confieri possit, paucis adverte, docebo: the brisk imperative adverte and the promise of a brief explanation make her plan sound organised, delivered like a general's briefing

venatum Aeneas unaque miserrima Dido in nemus ire parant: she builds the plan on the hunt already arranged; una places the pair together, and miserrima shows the narrator's pity for the victim of the plan
primos crastinus ortus extulerit Titan radiisque retexerit orbem: the grand description of sunrise times the plan precisely and contrasts the morning light with the darkness to come
his ego nigrantem commixta grandine nimbum … desuper infundam: the emphatic ego and the long delay before the verb infundam build up the storm Juno herself will pour down
dum trepidant alae saltusque indagine cingunt: the plan strikes while the huntsmen are busy with their nets; the hunters setting traps hint that Dido herself is the one being trapped
tonitru caelum omne ciebo: the harsh c and t sounds suggest the crash of thunder, and omne shows the scale of the plan
diffugient comites et nocte tegentur opaca: the confident future tenses foretell every step; the darkness that hides the companions makes the plan secret
speluncam Dido dux et Troianus eandem devenient: speluncam … eandem frames the two lovers, so the word order traps them in the cave together
conubio iungam stabili propriamque dicabo. hic hymenaeus erit: the formal language of a Roman wedding is ironic, and the blunt short sentence makes the ‘wedding’ sound more like a trap

essays.q: how does Virgil make Juno’s account of the storm and the ‘wedding’ ominous?
points: the storm will be black and mixed with hail
Juno will pour it down from above while the hunt is in full swing
thunder will fill the whole sky
the companions will flee and be hidden by dark night
Dido and Aeneas will be brought alone to the same cave
Juno promises a lasting marriage and declares that this will be the wedding
Venus does not oppose the plan and smiles at the trick she has seen through
features: his ego nigrantem commixta grandine nimbum: the storm is black and mixed with hail, a dark and violent setting for a ‘wedding’
dum trepidant alae saltusque indagine cingunt: the hunters setting their nets around the glades hint that Dido is the quarry, recalling the wounded deer
desuper infundam et tonitru caelum omne ciebo: desuper places the storm under divine control, and the harsh c and t sounds suggest the crash of thunder across the whole sky
diffugient comites et nocte tegentur opaca: the scattering companions and the dark night that hides them create an atmosphere of secrecy and danger
speluncam Dido dux et Troianus eandem devenient: speluncam … eandem encloses the pair, so the word order traps them together in the cave
adero et, tua si mihi certa voluntas, conubio iungam stabili propriamque dicabo: Juno uses the formal words of a Roman marriage; the promise of a lasting union (stabili) is ominously ironic
hic hymenaeus erit: the short, blunt sentence announces the ‘wedding’ like a sentence passed, a marriage held in a storm-dark cave
non adversata petenti adnuit: the litotes shows Venus' cool, calculating consent, with no concern for Dido
dolis risit Cytherea repertis: the goddess smiles at the trick she has seen through; the gods' amusement makes the tragedy ahead for Dido more ominous

essays.q: how does Virgil present Juno as confident and in control?
points: she replies at once and claims the task as her own
she tells Venus to listen and promises to explain in a few words how it can be done
she already knows what Aeneas and Dido plan to do the next day
she times her plan to the sunrise and the hunt
she will send the storm herself, pouring it down from above
she will stir the whole sky with thunder
she foretells exactly how the companions will scatter and be hidden in the dark
features: tum sic excepit regia Iuno: the epithet regia stresses her rank as queen of the gods as she takes up the conversation
mecum erit iste labor: mecum comes first, so Juno claims the whole task as her own, confident she can carry it out
nunc qua ratione quod instat confieri possit, paucis adverte, docebo: the imperative adverte and the brisk docebo make her speak like a commander giving orders, in no doubt that her plan will work
venatum Aeneas unaque miserrima Dido in nemus ire parant: she already knows the lovers' plans for the next day, which shows her in command of events
ubi primos crastinus ortus extulerit Titan: she fixes the exact time of her plan, at the next sunrise, a sign of careful control
his ego nigrantem commixta grandine nimbum … desuper infundam: the emphatic ego and the confident future infundam show her taking personal charge of the weather
dum trepidant alae saltusque indagine cingunt: she pictures the hunt in motion and times her storm to strike when everyone is busy, showing complete foresight
tonitru caelum omne ciebo: the hyperbole of omne and the harsh c and t sounds show her power over the whole sky
diffugient comites et nocte tegentur opaca: the run of future indicatives (diffugient, tegentur) states each outcome as certain, the voice of a goddess sure of her control

essays.q: how does Virgil make Dido’s despair vivid?
points: Dido, unhappy at heart, cannot sleep, and night reaches neither her eyes nor her heart
her anxieties redouble, and her love rises again and rages on a swell of anger
she turns things over in her heart and asks herself what she is to do
she pictures herself laughed at, begging the suitors she once rejected
she asks bitterly whether she should follow the Trojans and obey their orders, and whether they are grateful for her help
she realises they would not take her, a woman they despise, aboard their proud ships, and calls herself lost
she imagines fleeing alone among cheering sailors, or forcing her people to sea again after she barely tore them from Sidon
