features: at non infelix animi Phoenissa neque umquam solvitur in somnos: at non sets Dido apart from the sleeping world; the emphatic negatives non … neque umquam stress that she has no rest at all
oculisve aut pectore noctem accipit: sleep is denied to her eyes and her heart, so her sleeplessness seems total; enjambment of accipit drags the sentence on like the endless night
ingeminant curae rursusque resurgens saevit amor: ingeminant, ‘redouble’, and rursus … resurgens show her cares rising again and again; saevit, used of wild beasts and storms, makes her love savage
magnoque irarum fluctuat aestu: the sea imagery pictures her emotions as a stormy swell tossing her back and forth
en, quid ago?: the abrupt direct question in the present tense lets us hear her desperate thoughts as she speaks them
rursusne procos inrisa priores experiar, Nomadumque petam conubia supplex: inrisa and supplex show her imagining humiliation, the proud queen reduced to begging the suitors she rejected
quiane auxilio iuvat ante levatos et bene apud memores veteris stat gratia facti?: bitter sarcasm shows her sense of betrayal by the Trojans she once rescued

nescis heu, perdita, necdum Laomedonteae sentis periuria gentis?: self-address and the exclamation heu show a mind divided against itself; the heavy adjective Laomedonteae brands the Trojans as oath-breakers
sola fuga nautas comitabor ovantes?: sola is set against the cheering sailors (ovantes), a painful picture of her isolation
quos Sidonia vix urbe revelli, rursus agam pelago et ventis dare vela iubebo?: the last of her rhetorical questions closes every option; revelli recalls how hard it was to tear her people from Tyre

essays.q: how does Virgil present Dido’s thoughts about the choices open to her?
points: she begins by asking herself what she is to do
she imagines being laughed at as she begs the Numidian suitors she rejected so often
she considers following the Trojan fleet and obeying their every order
she asks whether the Trojans are grateful for the help she gave them
she sees that they would not let her, a hated woman, aboard their proud ships
she calls herself lost and recalls the broken oaths of Laomedon’s race
she pictures fleeing alone with the rejoicing sailors
she imagines making her own people put to sea again, though she could hardly tear them away from Sidon
features: en, quid ago?: the abrupt deliberative question in the present tense opens her debate with herself urgently, as if thinking aloud
rursusne procos inrisa priores experiar: the first choice, returning to her former suitors, is rejected at once; inrisa shows her fear of being laughed at
Nomadumque petam conubia supplex, quos ego sim totiens iam dedignata maritos?: supplex and totiens dedignata set her imagined begging against her past pride, so this choice seems humiliating
Iliacas igitur classes atque ultima Teucrum iussa sequar?: the second choice, following the Trojans, is framed as obeying their meanest orders (ultima iussa), which a queen cannot accept
quiane auxilio iuvat ante levatos et bene apud memores veteris stat gratia facti?: bitter irony shows her thinking the Trojans ungrateful, so this choice collapses too

quis me autem, fac velle, sinet ratibusve superbis invisam accipiet?: she answers her own question; the parenthesis fac velle and the word invisam show that even if she wished it, she would not be welcome
nescis heu, perdita, necdum Laomedonteae sentis periuria gentis?: self-address shows her mind arguing with itself, and the allusion to Laomedon brands all Trojans as liars
quid tum? sola fuga nautas comitabor ovantes?: the clipped quid tum? hurries her on to the next option; sola set against ovantes makes it painful
an Tyriis omnique manu stipata meorum inferar: the final choice, leading her people after the Trojans, is pictured on a large scale (omnique manu) to show its impossibility
quos Sidonia vix urbe revelli, rursus agam pelago: revelli recalls how hard it was to tear her people from Tyre; the series of rejected questions leaves her no way out

essays.q: how does Virgil convey Dido’s bitterness and guilt?
points: she believes the Trojans would never let her, a woman they despise, aboard their proud ships
she calls herself lost and brands the Trojans as oath-breakers, the race of Laomedon
she imagines fleeing alone among the cheering sailors
she cannot ask her people, whom she barely tore away from Sidon, to set sail again
she orders herself to die as she deserves and end her grief with the sword
she blames her sister for giving way to her tears and throwing her to her enemy
she wishes she had lived free of marriage like a wild creature
she admits she has broken her vow to Sychaeus’ ashes
features: quis me autem, fac velle, sinet ratibusve superbis invisam accipiet?: superbis and invisam express her bitterness at the proud Trojans who now hate her
nescis heu, perdita, necdum Laomedonteae sentis periuria gentis?: she turns on herself as perdita, then brands all Trojans as oath-breakers through the heavy adjective Laomedonteae
sola fuga nautas comitabor ovantes?: the bitter picture of her alone among cheering sailors (sola … ovantes) sharpens her sense of humiliation
quin morere ut merita es, ferroque averte dolorem: the abrupt imperative passes sentence on herself; ut merita es shows her guilt, and the sword is presented as a cure for pain
tu lacrimis evicta meis, tu prima furentem his, germana, malis oneras: the anaphora of tu turns her bitterness on Anna; germana, in the middle of the accusation, shows love and resentment together
atque obicis hosti: obicis is a violent word, and hosti calls Aeneas an enemy, showing how bitter her feelings have become

non licuit thalami expertem sine crimine vitam degere more ferae: she regrets that she could not live free of marriage and blame; crimine shows her guilt, and more ferae envies a wild animal's innocence
tales nec tangere curas: she wishes she had never touched such troubles, a regret that blames her own choice
non servata fides cineri promissa Sychaeo: the anaphora of non with non licuit sets out what she has lost; ending on Sychaeo leaves the reader with the vow she has broken, the root of her guilt

essays.q: how does Virgil make Dido’s decision to die moving?
points: she pictures driving her people to sea again
she remembers that she could hardly tear them away from Sidon
she suddenly tells herself to die, as she deserves
she sees the sword as the way to end her grief
she turns on her sister, blaming her for giving way to her tears
she accuses her of loading her with suffering and throwing her to her enemy
she wishes she could have lived without marriage, like a wild creature
she ends by admitting that she broke her vow to Sychaeus
features: an Tyriis omnique manu stipata meorum inferar: her last possible choice is pictured on a grand scale, which only shows how impossible it is

quos Sidonia vix urbe revelli, rursus agam pelago et ventis dare vela iubebo?: revelli recalls the pain of leaving Tyre, and the pairing pelago et ventis makes another voyage feel exhausting, so every way out is closed

quin morere ut merita es, ferroque averte dolorem: the sudden imperative passes sentence on herself; ut merita es shows she believes she deserves death, and ferro presents the sword as a release from pain
tu lacrimis evicta meis, tu prima furentem: the anaphora of tu shows her turning, in pain, on the sister who gave way to her tears; furentem at the line end recalls her madness
his, germana, malis oneras atque obicis hosti: the affectionate germana inside the accusation is moving, showing love and blame together; hosti shows Aeneas now seen as an enemy
non licuit thalami expertem sine crimine vitam degere more ferae: her wish for a blameless life like a wild animal's is poignant; crimine shows the guilt driving her decision
tales nec tangere curas: she wishes she had never touched such cares, a regret that makes her decision more tragic
non servata fides cineri promissa Sychaeo: the anaphora non … non sets out what she has lost; cineri, ‘ashes’, is a touching reminder of her dead husband, and the speech ends on his name

essays.q: how does Virgil make this a dramatic turning point?
points: Dido orders herself to die by the sword, as she deserves
she blames her sister for giving way to her tears and throwing her to her enemy
she regrets that she could not live free of marriage and admits breaking her vow to Sychaeus
her great laments burst from her heart
meanwhile Aeneas, sure he will go, sleeps on the high stern with everything ready
the god appears to him again in a dream, with the same face as before
the figure looks exactly like Mercury, in voice, colouring, golden hair and youthful limbs
it seems to warn him once more
features: quin morere ut merita es, ferroque averte dolorem: Dido passes sentence on herself with a blunt imperative; the decision to die is made in a single line, which marks the turning point at once
tu lacrimis evicta meis, tu prima furentem: anaphora of tu turns her anger on Anna, so the moment of decision is charged with blame and bitterness
his, germana, malis oneras atque obicis hosti: the tender address germana sits inside violent verbs of loading and throwing, and Aeneas is now hosti, an enemy: her feelings have turned completely
non licuit thalami expertem sine crimine vitam degere more ferae: the comparison with a wild creature shows her longing for the innocence she can never recover, which seals her decision
non servata fides cineri promissa Sychaeo: the second non sentence ends her speech on Sychaeus' name, so her guilt over the broken vow is the last thing she says before the scene changes
tantos illa suo rumpebat pectore questus: hyperbole of tantos and the violent rumpebat present her grief as bursting out, a climax before the sudden shift of scene
Aeneas celsa in puppi iam certus eundi carpebat somnos: the abrupt cut to Aeneas, calm and sleeping on the high stern, sets the two at opposite poles at the decisive moment
iam certus eundi carpebat somnos rebus iam rite paratis: repeated iam and rite stress that his departure is settled and orderly, which makes the contrast with Dido's turmoil dramatic
huic se forma dei vultu redeuntis eodem obtulit in somnis: the sudden arrival of the god in a dream signals divine intervention, so the story turns again just as Dido has chosen death
vocemque coloremque et crines flavos et membra decora iuventae: polysyndeton (and the hypermetric -que) lingers on the god's appearance, making the vision vivid and building suspense before he speaks

essays.q: how does Virgil contrast Dido’s grief with Aeneas’ readiness to leave?
points: Dido regrets that she was not allowed to live free of marriage and its troubles
she admits that she has broken her vow to Sychaeus
her laments are great and burst from her heart
Aeneas, by contrast, is already certain that he will go
he is sleeping on the high stern
everything has already been properly prepared
the god appears to him in his sleep, looking exactly like Mercury, to warn him again
features: non licuit thalami expertem sine crimine vitam degere more ferae: Dido's wish to have lived like a wild creature, free of marriage, shows how much her grief is bound up with guilt and lost innocence
tales nec tangere curas: curas sums up her anguish; she wishes she had never been touched by such troubles, which Aeneas, by contrast, can set aside
non servata fides cineri promissa Sychaeo: anaphora of non and the closing name Sychaeo end her lament on the broken vow, so her grief is heavy with self-reproach
tantos illa suo rumpebat pectore questus: hyperbole of tantos and the violent rumpebat show grief bursting from her, in sharp contrast with the calm that follows
Aeneas celsa in puppi iam certus eundi: the immediate cut to Aeneas, placed high on the stern and certus, sure of going, contrasts his firm resolve with her turmoil
carpebat somnos rebus iam rite paratis: he sleeps peacefully while she cannot; rite suggests everything has been done properly, so his orderly readiness sharpens the pathos of her grief
iam certus eundi … rebus iam rite paratis: the repeated iam stresses that his preparations are already complete while she is still lamenting
huic se forma dei vultu redeuntis eodem obtulit in somnis: even the god comes to Aeneas in a calm dream, so the gods are on the side of his departure while Dido is left alone with her grief
vocemque coloremque et crines flavos et membra decora iuventae: the leisurely, polysyndetic description of the god's youthful beauty contrasts with the violent language of Dido's lament

essays.q: how does Virgil make Mercury’s warning urgent?
points: Mercury wakes Aeneas with a rebuke: he can sleep on at such a dangerous time
he calls the hero mad for failing to see the dangers or hear the favourable winds
he presents Dido as dangerous, plotting treachery and crime, set on dying
he describes her anger as shifting tides she keeps stirring up
he urges Aeneas to flee headlong while flight is still possible
he paints a picture of the harbour full of ships, torches and a shore ablaze if dawn finds Aeneas still there
he ends with a scornful judgement that a woman is always fickle and changeable, then vanishes into the night
features: nate dea, potes hoc sub casu ducere somnos: Mercury opens with a reproachful rhetorical question, reminding Aeneas of his divine birth and making his sleep look like dangerous carelessness
nec quae te circum stent deinde pericula cernis, demens, nec Zephyros audis spirare secundos: a string of questions, linked by nec … nec, piles up what Aeneas is failing to notice and builds urgency
pericula cernis, demens: the insult demens, 'madman', placed emphatically at the start of the line, jolts Aeneas awake and stresses how foolish delay would be
illa dolos dirumque nefas in pectore versat certa mori: Dido is presented as a threat; the alliteration of d in dolos dirumque and certa mori make her seem deadly and determined
variosque irarum concitat aestus: the metaphor of stormy tides of anger suggests danger that is powerful and unpredictable, so Aeneas must leave at once
non fugis hinc praeceps, dum praecipitare potestas: polyptoton of praeceps and praecipitare, with harsh p sounds, insists on headlong speed while there is still time

iam mare turbari trabibus saevasque videbis conlucere faces, iam fervere litora flammis: anaphora of iam and the vivid future picture of the sea churned with ships and the shore ablaze make the danger feel immediate
si te his attigerit terris Aurora morantem: the condition sets a deadline, dawn, so every moment of delay increases the danger
heia age, rumpe moras: short, clipped imperatives in everyday language hurry Aeneas on; the rhythm itself is urgent
varium et mutabile semper femina: the sweeping generalisation, with femina held over emphatically to the next line, warns that Dido may change at any moment, so he must not wait

essays.q: how does Virgil make this a dramatic account of the Trojans’ departure?
points: Aeneas is terrified by the sudden vision and tears himself from sleep
he drives his men on in headlong haste
he gives a rapid string of orders: wake up, man the benches, loose the sails
he explains that a god has spurred them on a second time to cut the ropes
he prays to the god, whoever he is, and promises joyful obedience
he draws his flashing sword and cuts the mooring ropes himself
all his men are seized by the same eagerness, abandon the shore and churn the sea to foam
features: tum vero Aeneas subitis exterritus umbris: tum vero marks a decisive moment, and exterritus with subitis conveys the shock that drives the sudden action

corripit e somno corpus sociosque fatigat praecipites: historic presents and the violent corripit make Aeneas' reaction instant, and praecipites, emphatic at the start of the line, conveys headlong haste
vigilate, viri, et considite transtris; solvite vela citi: a rapid string of imperatives in direct speech, with alliteration of v, shows Aeneas taking command and drives the action forward

deus aethere missus ab alto festinare fugam tortosque incidere funes ecce iterum instimulat: ecce and the vivid present instimulat make the divine command seem present and pressing, and iterum stresses its urgency
sequimur te, sancte deorum, quisquis es, imperioque iterum paremus ovantes: the prayer in the middle of the action adds solemnity, presenting the departure as joyful obedience to the gods
dixit vaginaque eripit ensem fulmineum: speech turns to action within the line, and fulmineum, held over to line 580, makes the drawn sword flash like lightning
strictoque ferit retinacula ferro: alliteration of f and r gives the stroke a harsh, decisive sound, and cutting the ropes is a dramatic symbol of breaking his ties with Carthage
idem omnes simul ardor habet, rapiuntque ruuntque: the shared ardour of omnes simul and the polysyndeton of two r-verbs capture the frantic rush of the whole crew
litora deseruere, latet sub classibus aequor: the sudden perfect deseruere makes the departure already complete, and the hyperbole of the sea hidden beneath the ships shows its scale
adnixi torquent spumas et caerula verrunt: the vivid verbs and steady rhythm convey the effort of the oarsmen as the fleet surges away

essays.q: how does Virgil create a sense of haste and danger in this passage?
points: Mercury warns that Dido is plotting treachery and crime and is set on dying
he urges Aeneas to flee headlong while he still can
he describes the sea churned up with ships and the shore ablaze with torches
he warns that this will happen if dawn finds Aeneas still lingering
he tells Aeneas to break off his delay, then vanishes into the black night
Aeneas, terrified, tears himself from sleep and rouses his men
he orders them to man the benches and loose the sails quickly, and prays to the god
features: illa dolos dirumque nefas in pectore versat certa mori: Mercury presents Dido as a danger; the alliteration of d and certa mori make her threat seem deadly and resolved
variosque irarum concitat aestus: the metaphor of stormy tides of anger suggests a danger that is rising and unpredictable
non fugis hinc praeceps, dum praecipitare potestas: the reproachful question and polyptoton of praeceps … praecipitare demand headlong flight while it is still possible
iam mare turbari trabibus saevasque videbis conlucere faces, iam fervere litora flammis: anaphora of iam and vivid images of churning sea and blazing shore make the danger seem imminent
si te his attigerit terris Aurora morantem: the warning sets dawn as a deadline, adding the pressure of time
heia age, rumpe moras: short, clipped imperatives drive the pace on and press Aeneas to act at once
sic fatus nocti se immiscuit atrae: the god's sudden disappearance into black night leaves an ominous atmosphere and a sense of danger
tum vero Aeneas subitis exterritus umbris corripit e somno corpus: Aeneas' terror and the violent, present-tense corripit show him springing into action at once
sociosque fatigat praecipites: vigilate, viri, et considite transtris; solvite vela citi: praecipites and the rapid series of imperatives, with citi, convey the haste of the departure
festinare fugam tortosque incidere funes ecce iterum instimulat: festinare fugam and the vivid present instimulat stress that the gods themselves are hurrying him away

essays.q: how does Virgil make this a dramatic account of the Trojans’ departure and Dido’s discovery of it?
points: Aeneas tears out his sword and cuts the mooring ropes
the Trojans rush to leave together, and the sea vanishes beneath the ships
dawn breaks calmly over the earth
Dido watches from her tower as the fleet sails away and the harbour stands empty
she beats her breast and tears her hair
she cries out to Jupiter that a foreigner has mocked her kingdom
she orders her people to take up weapons, bring fire and pursue the ships
features: dixit vaginaque eripit ensem fulmineum: speech turns instantly to action in the vivid present eripit, and fulmineum makes the sword flash like lightning
strictoque ferit retinacula ferro: the alliteration of f and r gives a harsh, decisive sound to the moment the ties with Carthage are cut
idem omnes simul ardor habet, rapiuntque ruuntque: polysyndeton and the two r-verbs convey the frantic, unanimous rush to leave
litora deseruere, latet sub classibus aequor: the abrupt perfect deseruere makes the shore abandoned in an instant, and the hyperbole of the hidden sea shows the scale of the departure
et iam prima novo spargebat lumine terras Tithoni croceum linquens Aurora cubile: the calm, mythological description of dawn slows the pace and creates a pause before the storm of Dido's discovery
regina e speculis ut primam albescere lucem vidit: the scene switches to Dido watching from her tower; regina stresses her royal status at the moment she is abandoned
aequatis classem procedere velis, litoraque et vacuos sensit sine remige portus: she takes in the departing fleet and the empty harbour one after another; vacuos and sine remige double the emptiness

terque quaterque manu pectus percussa decorum flaventesque abscissa comas: vivid physical gestures of mourning, with the beauty of decorum and flaventes set against the violence, make her grief dramatic
pro Iuppiter! ibit hic, ait et nostris inluserit advena regnis: the exclamation to Jupiter and the indignant question in direct speech, with the contemptuous advena, give her outburst force
ite, ferte citi flammas, date tela, impellite remos: a rapid series of imperatives in asyndeton conveys frenzied but futile commands, ending the passage at a climax

essays.q: how does Virgil convey the force of Dido’s grief and anger?
points: the calm description of dawn comes just before Dido’s discovery
from her watchtower she sees the light whiten and the fleet move off
she realises the shore and harbour are empty
she strikes her lovely breast again and again and tears her golden hair
she calls on Jupiter and asks whether Aeneas will really go
she calls him a foreigner who has mocked her kingdom
she pours out orders for weapons, fire and pursuit
features: et iam prima novo spargebat lumine terras Tithoni croceum linquens Aurora cubile: the calm, decorative description of dawn creates a pause, so the outburst of grief that follows strikes with greater force
regina e speculis ut primam albescere lucem vidit: Dido, the queen, watches from above as the truth dawns on her, which sets up her shock
vacuos sensit sine remige portus: vacuos and sine remige say the same thing twice, stressing the totality of her desertion and so the cause of her grief
terque quaterque manu pectus percussa decorum: the formal phrase terque quaterque and the repeated beating of her lovely breast make her grief intense and physical
flaventesque abscissa comas: tearing her golden hair, a traditional act of mourning, shows grief turning to self-violence
pro Iuppiter! ibit hic: the sudden exclamation in direct speech, with ibit placed for emphasis, expresses her outraged disbelief that he will really go
nostris inluserit advena regnis: the contemptuous advena reduces Aeneas to a foreigner, and inluserit shows her sense of being mocked, so grief turns to anger
non arma expedient totaque ex urbe sequentur, diripientque rates alii navalibus: angry rhetorical questions demanding pursuit show her fury seeking action
ite, ferte citi flammas, date tela, impellite remos: a rush of imperatives in asyndeton conveys the force and speed of her anger

essays.q: how does Virgil make Dido’s reaction to the departure of Aeneas powerful?
points: Dido sees the dawn, the fleet sailing away and the empty harbour
she beats her breast and tears her hair
she cries out to Jupiter against the foreigner who has mocked her
she demands that her people arm themselves and pursue the ships
she gives urgent orders for fire, weapons and oars
she suddenly stops and asks what she is saying and where she is
she addresses herself as unhappy Dido and recognises the impious deeds too late
features: regina e speculis ut primam albescere lucem vidit: the queen watches from her tower as dawn breaks, so the reader shares the moment the truth dawns on her

aequatis classem procedere velis, litoraque et vacuos sensit sine remige portus: she takes in the sailing fleet and the deserted harbour in turn; the doubled emptiness of vacuos and sine remige stresses her abandonment
terque quaterque manu pectus percussa decorum flaventesque abscissa comas: repeated blows to her lovely breast and the tearing of her golden hair make her grief vivid and physical
pro Iuppiter! ibit hic: the outraged exclamation and question, with ibit given emphasis, convey shock and disbelief
nostris inluserit advena regnis: calling Aeneas advena, a mere foreigner, and complaining that he has mocked her kingdom shows wounded pride as well as grief
non arma expedient totaque ex urbe sequentur: angry rhetorical questions summon the whole city to arms, showing grief turning into fury
ite, ferte citi flammas, date tela, impellite remos: four commands in asyndeton convey frantic urgency; the orders are useless, which adds pathos
quid loquor aut ubi sum quae mentem insania mutat: three short questions show her suddenly coming to her senses and recognising her own madness, a powerful shift of mood
infelix Dido, nunc te facta impia tangunt: she addresses herself in the third person as infelix, seeing her own tragedy from outside, which makes her reaction deeply moving

essays.q: how does Virgil convey the force of Dido’s anger?
points: Dido questions her own words and her sanity
she reproaches herself for trusting Aeneas when she gave him her throne
she mocks his pledged hand and his famous piety towards his gods and his father
she wishes she had torn his body apart and scattered it on the waves
she imagines killing his men and serving Ascanius to his father
she brushes aside the risk, since she was going to die anyway
she pictures burning the Trojan camp and destroying father, son and race, with herself on top
features: quid loquor aut ubi sum quae mentem insania mutat: a burst of short rhetorical questions shows a mind in turmoil, out of which her anger erupts
tum decuit, cum sceptra dabas: the bitter contrast of tenses, then and now, shows her anger at her own trust when she shared her kingdom with Aeneas
en dextra fidesque: the sarcastic exclamation en mocks the pledge of his right hand and his good faith, which she now despises

quem secum patrios aiunt portare penates, quem subiisse umeris confectum aetate parentem: anaphora of quem lists his famous acts of piety, and aiunt turns them into mere hearsay, so the praise becomes scorn
non potui abreptum divellere corpus et undis spargere: violent verbs in an angry rhetorical question, with spargere enjambed like the scattered body, show the savagery of her rage
non socios, non ipsum absumere ferro Ascanium: anaphora of non builds a list of victims, rising to Ascanius, held over to the start of the line for shocking emphasis
patriisque epulandum ponere mensis: the horrific idea of serving the son at his father's table shows how far her anger has gone
verum anceps pugnae fuerat fortuna. fuisset: she answers her own objection with a single defiant word, fuisset, which shows her anger sweeping aside reason
faces in castra tulissem implessemque foros flammis: the alliteration of f and the fire imagery in past unreal subjunctives show the destruction she imagines
natumque patremque cum genere exstinxem, memet super ipsa dedissem: polysyndeton sweeps up every generation, and the emphatic memet … ipsa shows she would have died in the destruction too

essays.q: how does Virgil make Dido’s prayer and the start of her curse solemn and powerful?
points: Dido calls on the Sun, who sees every deed on earth
she calls on Juno, witness of her torments
she calls on Hecate, the avenging Furies and the gods of dying Elissa
she commands the gods to hear her and turn their power on her wrongs
she accepts that fate may bring Aeneas to land
she wishes him to be harried by war and driven from his borders
she wishes him torn from Iulus, begging for help and watching his men die
features: Sol, qui terrarum flammis opera omnia lustras: the formal invocation of the Sun, who sees every deed, gives the prayer a solemn, cosmic scope
tuque harum interpres curarum et conscia Iuno: Juno is addressed as go-between and witness of Dido's torments, so the gods are called on as those who know her wrongs
nocturnisque Hecate triviis ululata per urbes: the eerie sound of ululata and the night-time crossroads give the invocation a dark, uncanny power
et Dirae ultrices et di morientis Elissae: polysyndeton extends the list of powers to the avenging Furies and the gods of the dying queen, building a rising sequence of invocations
accipite haec, meritumque malis advertite numen et nostras audite preces: three imperatives to the gods, in the formal language of prayer, make her demand for justice solemn
si tangere portus infandum caput ac terris adnare necesse est: the measured condition accepts fate before cursing, so the curse seems considered; infandum caput reduces Aeneas to an accursed head
et sic fata Iovis poscunt, hic terminus haeret: the solemn image of the boundary stone makes her acceptance of fate weighty, before she turns to curse

at bello audacis populi vexatus et armis, finibus extorris, complexu avulsus Iuli: a list of sufferings in curse language, with the pairing bello … et armis and the violent avulsus, gives the curse power
auxilium imploret videatque indigna suorum funera: the jussive subjunctives turn wishes into commands, and funera, held over to the next line, lands with heavy force

essays.q: how does Virgil show Dido’s thoughts turning to violent revenge?
points: Dido addresses herself as unhappy and regrets giving Aeneas her throne
she mocks the pledged hand and good faith of Aeneas
she sneers at the stories of his piety towards his gods and father
she imagines tearing his body apart and scattering it on the waves
she imagines killing his men and serving Ascanius at his father’s table
she dismisses the danger of the fight because she was going to die
she pictures setting fire to the Trojan ships and destroying their whole line, with herself on top
features: infelix Dido, nunc te facta impia tangunt: Dido's self-address and the pointed word impia show her bitterness beginning to turn outward against Aeneas
tum decuit, cum sceptra dabas. en dextra fidesque: the contrast of then and now and the sarcastic en mock the pledge of loyalty, preparing for her thoughts of revenge
quem secum patrios aiunt portare penates, quem subiisse umeris confectum aetate parentem: anaphora of quem and the sneering aiunt dismiss his piety, so she sees him as deserving punishment
non potui abreptum divellere corpus et undis spargere: the violent verbs divellere and spargere, with spargere enjambed, picture his body torn apart and scattered, the first of her savage fantasies
non socios, non ipsum absumere ferro Ascanium: anaphora of non builds a rising list of victims, with Ascanium held over for shocking emphasis
patriisque epulandum ponere mensis: the gerundive conjures the horror of a son served at his father's table, the darkest point of her revenge

verum anceps pugnae fuerat fortuna. fuisset: quem metui moritura: she brushes aside the risk with a single word, and moritura shows that facing death she fears nothing, which frees her to imagine violence
faces in castra tulissem implessemque foros flammis: past unreal subjunctives and the alliteration of f in a fire image show the destruction she wishes she had caused
natumque patremque cum genere exstinxem, memet super ipsa dedissem: polysyndeton sweeps away every generation, and memet … ipsa shows her thoughts of revenge merging with her own death

essays.q: how does Virgil make Dido’s curse powerful?
points: Dido accepts that fate may bring Aeneas to land
she curses him with war, exile and separation from Iulus
she wishes him to beg for help and see his men die undeserved deaths
she wishes him an unjust peace, an early death and no burial
she pours out her prayer as her last words, with her blood
she commands the Tyrians to hate Aeneas’ race for ever, with no love or treaties
she calls for an avenger to rise from her bones and for endless war between the peoples
features: si tangere portus infandum caput ac terris adnare necesse est: the curse opens with a measured condition, accepting fate, which makes what follows sound deliberate; infandum caput reduces Aeneas to an accursed head

at bello audacis populi vexatus et armis, finibus extorris, complexu avulsus Iuli: a list of sufferings, with the pairing bello … et armis and the violent avulsus, heaps up the penalties in the language of a formal curse
auxilium imploret videatque indigna suorum funera: jussive subjunctives turn wishes into commands, and funera, held over to the next line, lands with heavy force
nec, cum se sub leges pacis iniquae tradiderit, regno aut optata luce fruatur: even the peace he seeks becomes a punishment, iniquae turning his reward into humiliation
sed cadat ante diem mediaque inhumatus harena: the climax of the curse on Aeneas is an early death and an unburied body on the open sand, the worst disgrace a Roman could imagine
haec precor, hanc vocem extremam cum sanguine fundo: her last words are poured out like a libation with her blood, so her death seals the curse
tum vos, o Tyrii, stirpem et genus omne futurum exercete odiis: the apostrophe to the Tyrians widens the curse from one man to every generation of both peoples
nullus amor populis nec foedera sunto: the old future imperative sunto, in the language of law, gives her decree of eternal enmity solemn force

exoriare aliquis nostris ex ossibus ultor qui face Dardanios ferroque sequare colonos: the second-person address to an avenger not yet born, with fierce alliteration of f in face … ferroque, makes the curse reach into the future

litora litoribus contraria, fluctibus undas imprecor, arma armis: pugnent ipsique nepotesque: polyptoton sets word against word to act out the clash of nations, and the hypermetric final line makes the war seem endless

essays.q: how does Virgil make Dido’s curse on Aeneas himself terrible?
points: Dido accepts that the fates of Jupiter may bring Aeneas to land
she calls him a cursed creature
she wishes him to be harried by the war and weapons of a bold people
she wishes him driven from his borders and torn from Iulus
she wishes him to beg for help and see his men die undeserved deaths
she wishes him an unjust peace and no enjoyment of his kingdom
she wishes him to die before his time and lie unburied in the sand
features: si tangere portus infandum caput ac terris adnare necesse est: Dido calmly accepts that fate will bring him to land, which makes the curse that follows seem deliberate and binding
infandum caput ac terris adnare: refusing to name Aeneas, she calls him an accursed head, a term from formal curses, which shows her loathing
et sic fata Iovis poscunt, hic terminus haeret: the solemn image of the boundary stone stresses the fixed destiny that she will now fill with suffering
at bello audacis populi vexatus et armis: the pairing of near synonyms bello … et armis doubles the threat of war against him
finibus extorris, complexu avulsus Iuli: exile and the violent separation from his son, conveyed by avulsus, strike at what Aeneas holds most dear
auxilium imploret videatque indigna suorum funera: jussive subjunctives turn wishes into commands; he must beg for help and watch his men die, with funera held over for emphasis
nec, cum se sub leges pacis iniquae tradiderit, regno aut optata luce fruatur: even peace becomes humiliation through iniquae, and he is denied the reign and the light he longs for
sed cadat ante diem mediaque inhumatus harena: the curse ends with an early death and an unburied body lying on the open sand, a terrible disgrace that closes the sentence with finality

essays.q: how does Virgil convey the lasting hatred Dido calls for between the two peoples?
points: Dido presents her words as her last prayer, poured out with her blood
she turns to the Tyrians and commands them to hate Aeneas’ whole race
she asks for this hatred as a gift to her ashes
she forbids any love or treaties between the peoples
she calls for an avenger to rise from her bones and pursue the Trojans with fire and sword
she wants the conflict now and in every age to come
she calls for shore against shore, sea against sea, weapon against weapon, for them and their descendants
features: haec precor, hanc vocem extremam cum sanguine fundo: her last words are poured out like a libation with her blood, so her death gives the curse its power to last
tum vos, o Tyrii, stirpem et genus omne futurum exercete odiis: the apostrophe to the Tyrians and the sweep of stirpem et genus omne futurum extend the hatred to every future generation
cinerique haec mittite nostro munera: hatred becomes an offering to her ashes, and munera held over to the start of the line gives the strange gift emphasis
nullus amor populis nec foedera sunto: the legal form sunto decrees permanent enmity, ruling out any love or treaty between the peoples
exoriare aliquis nostris ex ossibus ultor: the direct address to an unborn avenger rising from her bones makes the hatred outlive her and reach into the future
qui face Dardanios ferroque sequare colonos: the harsh alliteration of f in face … ferroque and the verb of pursuit present the future war as relentless
nunc, olim, quocumque dabunt se tempore vires: time words in asyndeton stretch the hatred across all ages, with no end in sight
litora litoribus contraria, fluctibus undas imprecor, arma armis: polyptoton sets each word against another form of itself, so the clashing words act out the endless conflict of the two nations
pugnent ipsique nepotesque: the final wish that they and their descendants fight, in a hypermetric line that runs on beyond its end, makes the hatred seem never-ending
